On section 38,

I would make a suggestion in reference to this matter of an audit. I would suggest that section 33 be amended so that there will he at the commencement of each year an audit made by a chartered accountant, and that he shall append to this statement that is to be made to the minister his certificate that this is a correct statement.

The suggestion that there shall be an examination by a chartered accountant is well worthy of consideration, but it must be distinctly understood that the accountant acts for the bank and not for the government. We do not wish to assume responsibility for inspecting these organizations at all. It would be proper that they should by their own by-laws cause an audit to be made by a chartered accountant. I think the suggestion is well worthy of consideration, and I will note it.
I do not mean that the department shall assume any responsibility for this audit. This section 38 would operate to subject the accountant to punishment if the certificate were incorrect.
Yes. I beg to move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.

Before the committee rises I would ask the hon. Minister of Finance to revert to section 9. Provision is made that the organization must be completed and that the certificate of the treasury board permitting the bank to carry on business shall be issued within a year from the date of the letters patent incorporating the bank, and also that in the event of the bank not obtaining a certificate

from the treasury hoard within that time the letters patent of the corporation and all rights shall cease. Would it not be wise to make some provision to revive what had been done without going through the whole procedure again. It is customary for a chartered bank in such a case as that to come to the House of Commons and ask for an extension of time. If there were some simple provision to that made here it might be the means of reviving the work that had been commenced, but had not been consummated within a year.

In the case of a chartered bank they would have to come to parliament and get an extension. In this case all they would have to do would be to make application to the Governor in Council for letters patent to be renewed and as the Governor in Council is always on hand there would not be very much delay.
I thought there was no provision made here for a renewal ?

House in committee on Bill (No. 200) respecting the inspection and sale of seeds. -The Minister of Agriculture.

Mr. Chairman, I think, perhaps, before this Bill is proceeded with section by section, that you will allow me to say a few words in general explanation of it. When the Bill was first introduced I was asked for an explanation, and I gave a very short one which satisfied the House at that time. But, I think I may say. this is a Bill involving a very considerable question, and one which is of very considerable importance to the agricultural community of this country. Therefore, it may not be out of place on my part to say a few words in regard to the events which have led up to the introduction of this Bill. Every one who is interested in agriculture knows well the great quantity of weeds that exist in our cultivated lands. I am well within the mark in saying that one of the greatest difficulties that our farmers have to contend with is in fighting the battle against weeds. A great deal of the best farm land is well cultivated and we have clean fields, and clean crops, but it is a deplorable fact that in certain lands there are a great number of bad weeds. At agricultural meetings throughout the country, Mr. HENDERSON.
this question has constantly come up and the speakers are frequently being asked how the weeds may be dealt with, and as to how new weeds come to be introduced. This has led to a very thorough discussion with reference to the control of the sale of seeds in order to secure that weed seeds should not be distributed with good seeds. I do not say that this is the only way in which weeds are distributed, but at the same time the attention of those interested in agricultural progress having been called to the question, investigation was had to ascertain to what extent weeds were being distributed through the ordinary sale of seeds. I undertook, as Minister of Agriculture, to start an investigation into this question two .years ago. I Secured the services of Mr. Clarke, who is a graduate of Guelph college, and who had given considerable attention to this subject. After thoroughly discussing the question with Prof. Robertson, we established what is commonly known as a seed laboratory for the testing of seeds and the investigation of all matters concerning them. This is a machinery which has been established in other countries, but it had never before been attempted in Canada. We secured samples of the ordinary seeds of commerce and we found a startling condition of affairs. While a great many of the seeds sold by the merchants and even by the smaller store keepers were quite good, there was found to be a very considerable proportion which were largely adulterated with weed seeds and with the seeds of plants which were not those supposed to be purchased. There was-also a large proportion of the seeds which were true to name, but which were not germinable. This latter defect is a comparatively trifling one, although serious enough in many samples which we obtained. But the distribution of the seeds of noxious weeds to farmers who believe they are buying goods seeds is a most serious matter and it conduces to inflict almost incalculable loss on the farmers. When you reflect that a farmer does not get the results of his sowing for nearly a year, and that if' the seed is bad he loses a whole year's work, you will see that it is a very serious blow to agricultural operations. It is still worse when he finds that instead of sowing his land with the seeds of what should turn out to be a profitable crop, he has been sowing the seeds of noxious and pestiferous weeds which may take him years to eradicate. One can well understand the incalculable loss inflicted on the farmers of the country in that way. In other countries efforts have been made to protect the farmers from the results of the trade in bad or impure or imperfect seeds. In England, in Germany, in Switzerland and in other countries, attention has been directed to this matter, and various forms of legislation have been adopted. In some of the states of the Union they have recognized the magnitude of the evii, and they have tried to lessen it by

legislation. In Manitoba, and I think the North-west Territories, various ordinances have been adopted, but in Canada there has been no general attempt up to the present time to deal with this matter at all. I have become fully satisfied that the time has arrived when in the interests of the farmers of the country it is necessary that this parliament should try to protect them in their business in this regard, and to minimize as much as possible the evils which have resulted from the condition of affairs I have described.

speakername: The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE. (Hon. Sydney Fisher).

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when you left the Chair, at six o'clock, I was explaining shortly what had led up to the introduction of the Bill now before the committee. I need not again go over that ground, except to state that this Bill is for the purpose of protecting farmers and others who purchase seeds from paying for what they do not intend to buy, and and from having sold to them under the name of good seeds the seeds of noxious and pernicious weeds. For many years back, at public meetings in which agricultural subjects have been discussed amongst the farmers of the land, constant inquiries with regard to the distribution of weeds in the country, the foulness of our laud, and the purity of the seeds sold by the trade, have been made of the speakers and the officials of the various agricultural departments who have been present at those meetings. These questions aroused such interest throughout the country that they seemed worthy of a thorough investigation, and some two years ago the officers of my department took up the matter with me. We concluded to hold an investigation, for the purpose of which I was able to secure the services of Mr. Clarke, who is now in charge of the seed laboratory here, and who had a good deal of training in this direction at Guelph, and in other ways. The result was the discovery of a condition of affairs which at first sight was rather startling. It was found, not only, that a great many of the seeds sold to the farmers were infertile or not germinable, but also that great quantities of the seeds of noxious weeds were included in the sample? for sale. We made arrangements to test thoroughly the samples of seeds so as to see just what their quality was, as gathered from all over the country. I may say that the samples obtained were generally from small dealers who sold direct to the farmers, and I daresay would be hardly entirely representative of the trade in seeds on the part of the best seed-producers in Canada. No doubt a great many of the best known seed firms in Canada sell direct to the farmers without the in-203
tervention of local dealers or salesmen, and I dare say that if a large number of samples of their seeds were to be tested, their average quality would be found to be much higher than the average quality of the samples we collected. Still, the samples we collected were those of the seeds which are sold to the farmers of the country in the ordinary course of trade, and therefore they do fairly represent the class of goods which the average farmer is obtaining and paying for. The samples obtained, as was stated in the bulletin issued last year on this subject, showed two or three things very markedly : first, that in many instances a large proportion of the seeds sold were not germinable-would not grow. That is a comparatively minor fault, although the investigation showed that the farmers were buying and paying for a great deal that was of no value.	Next, it showed
that in the samples of seeds a large proportion were not what they were represented to be, but included not only infertile seeds, but also dirt and foulness of various kinds. That, too, was a bad enough thing ; but it was not so great a hurt to the farmer as the greater wrong of selling the seeds of noxious weeds. In this the farmer suffers a loss which is most incalculable. He gets not only what is of no value to him, but what is going to cause immense loss, very likely for years, and not only to himself, but to all his neighbours in the locality in which he lives, for it may be but a short time before that noxious weed possesses a great portion of the land in which it is sown. There is no doubt that by means of the sale of seeds in Canada a considerable number of noxious weeds have been spread in parts of the country where previously they wrcre not known at all. Once estabished, they have spread over the land and have possessed it to a large extent. The condition of affairs seems to me to call for a remedy, and I believe the only effective remedy is legislation by the parliament of Canada dealing with this trade. Far be it from me to wish to interfere with the trade more than is absolutely necessary in the interest of those whom we desire to protect. I would be sorry to interfere in any way with legitimate trade, and I do not believe that this Bill, as proposed, with such modifications in it as the current of discussion may bring about, will interfere with legitimate trade. But I am desirous that this Bill should be so framed, as to interfere with illegitimate trade, so as to protect the purchasers of seeds from being imposed upon, either intentionally or unintentionally, by people who are handling seeds for sale in the country. Some may think-my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) may take this ground-that this is too paternal legislation. The hon. gentleman has accused me of introducing grandfatherly legislation. Well, I can endure the taunt from my hon.



friend if I place in the hands of the farmer machinery which is going to have the effect of protecting his fields from the introduction of noxious weeds, enabling him more clearly and easily to ascertain the exact value of what he is purchasing, and providing him with a remedy against the person who is selling him so evil a thing as impure, adulterated or ungerminable seeds for sowing on his land. I do not wish at all to claim every detail of this Bill as being perfect. I may say that the Bill has been drawn after careful study and investigation, not of one mouth or a few months, but of a couple of years, and it has been drawn after more or less consultation with seedsmen as well as farmers. I fully appreciate that there are some provisions in the Bill which the trade object to-some provisions which perhaps can be so modified as not to interfere with the trade as much as they appear on the service to do. I should be glad of suggestions which would make the Bill more perfect in that respect, so long as its essential purpose is not defeated or interfered with. I may say that a few weeks ago I received a deputation of the seedsmen of Canada, who on the introduction of this Bill learned something of its provisions, and came here to discuss with me its details. In that discussion they made propositions and pointed out provisions which they thought unduly interfered with their trade. I would be only too glad to have a thorough discussion of these points in committee, with the view of making such modifications in the Bill as to meet the views of the trade without affecting its primary object. I think that can best be done by threshing out the details of the Bill in the Committee of the Whole. I do not for a moment wish the committee to suppose that in every detail this Bill must pass or even should pass just as it is printed. After discussion, I shall be prepared to accept some amendments, which the House may deem desirable, or may possibly propose some, and I should like to have a most complete discussion. I am satisfied that the agricultural interests of Canada require a Bill of this kind. During last winter and fall, we had pretty thorough discussions of this subject at the meetings of the farmers' institutes all over the country, and my views were pretty fairly endorsed. In some cases formal resolutions were adopted and forwarded me, and in other cases the institute workers and speakers reported that the meetings they addressed were strongly in favour of legislation in this direction. No definite instructions were sent me because the meetings seemed to think that the officers in my department, with the information at their hands, would be able to frame a satisfactory measure. I might say that legislation in the United States and England and on the continent of Europe has been studied in order that we

might obtain from it some guidance in the framing of this Bill. We have also studied the results of seed testings in the different countries in order to see what might be necessary for the protection of the farmers in the seed trade. I am sorry that to-night my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Bruce) is not here. 1 hoped he would have been here as I told him last week I would have to take this Bill up on the first occasion when it was reached, but as he is head of one of the largest seed firms in this country and consequently deeply interested in this measure, I shall not ask to have the Bill moved out of committee until my hon. friend is present to give ns the benefit of his advice.
On section 2,
This Act shall come Into operation on the first day of September, 1903.

It has been represented to me that the seedsmen have, to a large extent, laid in their supplies for the coming season, and it would be impossible for them to carry on their trade, under the provisions of tills Act. without having longer warning. I shall let this clause stand a little while with the intention of putting in a later date than the 1st of September. It cannot come into operation the 1st of July this year, and the first of September next will be perhaps a little too soon for the trade to adapt itself to new conditions. The probability is I will make the date the 1st of July next year, but shall let the clause stand until I have some expression of opinion on the subject from members of the committee.

I would suggest that this Bill should not come into force until next year. It is rather a new thing to have the seed trade governed in the way the hon. minister wishes. I think it a very proper measure. If the Bill can be worked out, I think it will be in the interests of the seed trade and the seed-growers. The first of September, however, will be too soon to have it come into force. The seed will be harvested, threshed, and probably in the market for sale about the 1st of August. Under the circumstances, it would be almost impossible for the trade to offer seed such as this Bill calls for by the 1st of September, and the hon. minister would do better not to bring the Bill into operation before next year. In the meantime the discussion could go on and serve as notice to the trade that it would become operative next year.

So I think there is no doubt that it would be quite easy for the seed dealers of this country to live up to the provisions of this clause, and, in selling goods, not to sell seeds containing these weeds. There is a weed Which I see prevailing pretty extensively in the province of Quebec, and which is coming into eastern Ontario. It is a tall weed with a handsome purple flower. What is it ?
At What time is it in flower ?
It is in flower now.
Is it not a blue flower blooming close to the stalk of a large branching weed ?

Yes.
, The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE. That is what we call chicory. It is pretty prevalent in the province of Quebec.

Is it difficult to eradicate ?
The Minister of agriculture, i
think not if it is taken properly. It is not a weed the seeds of which we ever find in samples of seeds as sold.
There is a very bad weed we call switch grass. The hon. minister ought to stop the sale of that also.

My hon. friend (Mr. McGowan) will see that the seed of switch grass is not one of those seeds which it is at all difficult to detect. It can easily be removed from clover or alsike seed by fanning. So it is never mixed in with these seeds as sold. This is directed particularly against those seeds which the^ ordinary farmer buying seeds cannot easily distinguish. But the seed which my hon. friend speaks of, any farmer would observe if it were present among timothy or clover seed that he intended to buy.

But the hon. gentleman has included mustard, which is quite a large seed and easily detected, and wild oats also. I suppose that this Bill is intended to regulate the sale of turnip seed and rape seed, not grass seed only ?
Yes.
I think it would be better to include switch grass, which is one of the worst weeds we have.

In discussing this clause of the Bill, I think we must read it along with section 6, in order to properly understand what the minister proposes to do. Section 3 provides :
No person shall sell, or offer, expose or have in his possession for sale, for the purpose of seeding, any seeds of cereals, grasses, clovers, forage plants or vegetables, unless they are free from seeds of the following weeds:
And section 6 provides :
The provisions contained in this Act shall not apply to
(a.) Any person growing or selling seeds for the purpose of food, or,
(b.) Any person selling seeds direct to merchants to be cleaned a.nd graded before being offered for sale for the purpose of seeding.
In my previous criticism of the hon. minister's course one might have thought that I considered the minister too much inclined to paternalism in dealing with the farmers, having their products inspected at every turn. I may say that in this case he is not quite paternal enough. To my mind he is going about this whole matter in a wrong way, and I trust he will excuse me for saying so. Had he commenced at the root of the matter, instead of taking the seed after it is threshed and put upon the market, I think he would have accomplished a great deal more. We know very well that throughout the province of Ontario-and I

assume it is very much the same in every province-all the farms are not fouled with noxious weeds. You will find farmers who are careful, who have been careful for a long series of years, and upon whose farms practically none of these weeds are to be found. But other farms you will find literally covered-such farms as we often see travelling through the country on the railroad. One weed, that with the yellow flower, wild mustard, is observable in many parts of the country. To my mind the minister should rather have taken the other view, and made provision in his Bill that only from clean farms should seeds be sold for seeding purposes-I mean clover or grass seed-and put a penalty upon any farmer who would sell seeils for sowing that were produced on a farm that was known to be fouled with noxious weeds.
I can quite understand that the hon. minister would accomplish something if he would proceed in that way. A man who has a farm literally covered with wild mustard should not be permitted to sell seed to his neighbour, or sell it to a seed merchant to be sold again, because it would be sure to foul other farms as it had fouled his own. Surely if the question of seed can be dealt with at all, we could control it by preventing the sale from the farms where it is known that these noxious weeds are growing, and only make it legal for a man to sell seed for sowing purposes off a farm that he knows to be clean and free from weeds. 1 speak, of course, with reference to Canadian seeds, to seeds produced on Canadian farms. We could not in that way control imported seeds, and I regret very much that we are obliged to import so large a quantity. 1 fail to see why we should not produce, for example, all" the clover and timothy in this country that we require. There is a considerable quantity produced in certain sections of the country, and perhaps if there was more encouragement given to those who produce a pure seed, there would be more seed grown in the country. No doubt we import a considerable amount of seed, and possibly some portion of that is exported again. I trust that we are not sowing so much seed imported from the United States as at first we might think. At any rate so far as Canadian seeds are concerned, I would like the minister to look at the matter in this light that instead of imposing a fine upon the man who is selling the seeds and who of necessity has to take his chances in buying them, he would take some steps to secure the seed merchant from the necessity of cleaning these seeds by preventing the man who has a farm fouled with noxious seeds from taking his seed to market and selling it to the seed merchant. That is my general idea of the whole question, and I think more can be accomplished in that way than by the enactment he is providing for.

My hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson), I am glad to see, thinks that some paternalism at all events is useful, and lie is willing to endorse a certain dose of it.
I am in hopes that before we get through with this discussion, he will agree with me that the provisions of this Bill are about the right kind of paternalism that we require. But my hon. friend has proposed a much more drastic measure than I am proposing, and one which I have not felt that I could propose to the House, either in the hope of carrying it or of making it effective if carried. After all, I am not quite sure that even if it were carried, it would be entirely fair. My hon. friend has instanced wild mustard in the grain crops of the country. It is far too prevalent, I know ; but my hon. friend may not know, though I think he does, that mustard seed can be very speedily separated from grain. A man might have his farm foul with mustard, and still be able to sell a perfectly clean sample of oats, or barley or wheat, cleaning it by a very simple manipulation before lie puts it on the market. As a matter of fact there are some seeds very easy to separate, and others very difficult to get out of samples to be sold. The seed merchants, people who handle seeds, have facilities and have apparatus for cleaning grain, and it is part of their business to do that work. The ordinary farmer who raises grain, who raises clover or timothy, has not generally got those facilities, it is not part of his business, and it would be a great hardship to require him to do it. The seed merchant need not buy from the farmer whose land he knows to be fouled with bad seed, and if he did not, those farmers would very soon cease to attempt placing their grain on the market at all, but would sell their product for feed or feed it at home. I think the provisions of the Bill will accomplish more than the proposition of my hon. friend would do, even if it could be passed in this House.

The provisions of this Bill are of considerable importance. We cannot go through large portions of the province of Ontario without observing that there is a large mixture of foul seed in the grain of the country. I think I never saw so much mustard in the fields of Canada as I have seen this year. Still, it appears to me that there are some things in this Bill that will bear with undue harshness upon the dealers in seeds. I have seen samples of various kinds of weeds, some of which are mentioned in this Bill, and from what I can learn, no means have yet been discovered of separating completely those foul seeds from out of the grain ; unless they are different in size and conformation they will go through the screen, and that makes the grain worthless. This Bill makes it illegal for a man to have bad seeds for sale,

and in that respect it is rather hard on dealers in seeds who may not be experts themselves, and may not be able to detect the various foul seeds that are found, especially in clover. A man may buy seed believing it to be all right and have it in his possession for sale. I doubt if any dealers in seeds in Ontario are willing to buy any seed for sale, or for the purpose of sowing, knowing it to be mixed with the seed of weeds. But they may become possessors of such mixed seed innocently, and by this measure they are liable to a heavy fine. If in some way a measure could be made to reach those who knowingly have weeds growing upon their farm, and who sell this foul seed with their grain, it would be a fairer measure than it stands at present.

I fully sympathize with the object of this Bill. I think anything workable that can be passed in the direction indicated by the Bill, is desirable legislation. But I fear that in order to give effect to this Bill in certain quarters, the Minister of Agriculture has gone so far as to make it unduly harsh in another quarter. It is a very difficult thing, I admit, to draw the line between who is and who is not a seller of seeds. The hon. gentleman will see that he necessarily includes every farmer in the country in some of the provisions of this rather drastic legislation. Now the hon. gentleman as a farmer himself knows that there is a good deal of seed of the various classes mentioned here that never goes through the hands of either the wholesale or the retail dealer. He knows very well, and he has said as much this evening, that there are certain classes o'f foul seed which get among the farmers' grain without any fault of theirs. If they do discover them they have no means of eradicating them and therefore it would be a very great hardship if you were to enforce sections 3 and 4. If I may be permitted to refer in advance to section 4, I would call attention to the fact that it provides that:
No person shall sell, or offer, expose or have In his possession for sale any seeds of timothy, red clover or afsike, or any mixture of the said seeds, unless each and every receptacle, package, sack or bag containing such seeds is marked in a plain and indelible manner.
(a.) With the initials of the Christian names, and the full surname and address of the wholesale or retail seller.
Every farmer in the country who exchanges with or sells to his neighbour which is the most common practice will be liable to the penalty of this law. It is a common practice for farmers to go around amongst each other hunting for seed. Thus, by reason of these foul seeds being difficult to discover and by reason of the farmer having no means of clearing them out, it would be a great hardship to subject them to the provisions of this Bill. Then, the hon. minister knows perfectly well that no farmer would have the receptacles, bags, boxes, or packages, which are designated here. He does not have such things. He has only the ordinary grain bags that he uses. My hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) who is a lawyer says : ' Let him ge them. It is not an easy thing for the farmer to get them.' That is not the custom of the farmer. It is entirely out of his routine of work. The farmer simply sells his grain or exchanges it with his neighbour and if this Bill were applied every one of these persons would come under its provisions. It seems to me that the hon. minister ought to confine the provisions of this Bill to persons engaged as dealers. It would greatly minimize the evil effects that would come from sowing foul seeds and it would give relief to a class of persons who will find it difficult to comply with the law. Even in the exceptions the farmer is not relieved from its provisions :
Any person selling seeds direct to merchants to be cleaned and graded before being offered for sale for the purpose of seeding.
AVell, he cannot tell. He has practically no exemption there beyond the exemption that applies if he sells for the purpose of food. I venture to say that in many cases there is no inquiry made as to whether grain is sold for food or not. The farmer goes into market with a load of grain. In many cases seed dealers are shippers as well. They ship large quantities that they do not make any pretense of selling for seed at all. Yet, immense quantities are bought for seed and the farmer sells in the ordinary way to a grain buyer who is also a seed dealer. He does not sell it for seed; he sells it generally. He simply sells it and he is liable unless he can prove that he did not sell it for seed. The provisions of section 4, it seems to me, impose impossible penalties upon the farmer.

I must disagree entirely with the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) in respect to this matter. I see no reason in the world why farmers who sell seed should not be put under the same penalty as a dealer who sells impure seed. I think this Bill is in the right direction and that the hon. Minister of Agriculture is to be congratulated upon having produced such a Bill. Let any man go through the country, through Ontario, or through the maritime provinces and he will find nearly every farm he passes is polluted with these foul seeds. This is becoming a very serious matter, and I think this step has not been taken one day too soon. Of course, there will be hardships. There are always hardships, but private interests must give way to public good and I think the farmer should be put upon the same plane as the dealer in connection with this matter. As to what the hon. member for Bothwell has said about the farmer selling his load of grain being

liable, be is not liable if be sells that grain generally without selling it for seed. It is impossible to interpret the Act in the way the hon. member for Bothwell does. He is not liable unless he sells his grain for seed and he should be exactly under the same penalties as the ordinary dealer if he sells it for seed.

Mr. Chairman, I think it will be conceded that one of the most valuable products we have in Canada is our seed grain, especially in Ontario. By degrees, in the years to come the trade thinks, at any rate, that a large quantity if not the most of the wheat produced in Canada will be grown on the western prairies. This will make the seed crop-the grass and clover crop of Ontario-more valuable from year to year and the area' will constantly extend. Under these circumstances I can readily see that it is absolutely necessary that some law should be put in force in order to regulate the sale of such an important farm product as seeds. The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) said that the hon. minister should go farther and provide that the farmer should clean his soil and that he should cut the noxious weeds or if possible pull them out. I understand that in Ontario we already have a law dealing with noxious weeds not only on the roadway but on the farms, but I am told it is not lived up to. I think, perhaps, that may be on account of the fact that the responsibility of inforcing the law is placed upon the municipalities and the municipalities do not accept their responsibility in that connection. The three great seeds which are most largely grown in Ontario are red clover, alsike and timothy. I have been told that we, in Ontario, are the largest producers of alsike clover in the world. Standing in that position it is absolutely necessary that we should have some standard of excellence with the view of bringing this product up to the finest seed that can be grown in the world. We grow some very fine samples, but when it comes a year in which weeds are prolific and when they grow rapidly they oftentimes fill up the crop and unless they are cut down at a particular season of the year, or unless they can try and cut them from the top of the clover, there is apt to be a quantity of foul seed with the clover seed. One seed that is found in nearly all of it is the mustard. Particularly will mustard be found in red clover and alsike. I have seen samples of timothy with mustard in, but it is a rare tiling to get mustard in timothy because in cleaning it the mustard seed runs back over the sieve and the timothy drops through. Timothy seed will have an occasional mustard but it will have other seeds which are a very great hindrance to the growing crop. The ox-eye daisy has been mentioned. This seed it very common in timothy. We have also a little wild flax occasionally. I handle Mr. FOWLER.
seeds myself and I often see samples of seeds with ' thistle ' in them. It seemsi to be very common in the ' timothy,' but I do not think you can get any thistle in alsike or in red clover. No one can travel throughout this country and look at the grasses and the clover without seeing in some cases large quantities of those noxious weeds. Somebody must be responsible for that. The provincial legislation on the subject does not appear to work, but a law like this which would get at the root of the evil will, I believe, be acceptable to the trade and to the farmers. I would, however, suggest that in line 8 of clause 3 after the word ' seeding ' there should be inserted the words ' within the Dominion of Canada.'
No person shall sell or offer, expose or have in his possession for sale for the purpose of seeding within the Dominion of Canada, any seeds, &c.
In connection with these seeds that are brought to the man who wholesales them, he cleans the seeds as a rule and he sells the best. At certain seasons of the year he has a lot of stuff left which you may call ' cleanings,' and these are shipped out of the country. I am told by a seedsman that they are not sold within the country, but they are exported because there is a demand for them in the old land where they are used for mixing purposes. I am told that a certain amount of weeds are put with the other grasses, but that they cannot grow some of the seeds which we have here to the perfection they do in this country, and that under these circumstances these cleanings find a good market outside of Canada.
I would therefore suggest that the clause be amended as I have indicated. If the amendment be made, the seedsman could not have these seeds in his possession for sale; he could have them for export purposes, but he could not have them for sale for domestic purposes, whereas under the Bill as it now stands he could not have them in. his possession for any purpose. He would therefore have to burn this stuff which has value for export. These ' cleanings ' are not shipped out of the country on consignment. It is not like the apple trade in that respect. Apples are shipped to Liverpool or Glasgow on consignment and sold at public auction, but I am informed that there is not a bushel of seed shipped out of Canada on commission. If we prevent this stuff being sold in Canada, there should be no reason for a man having to destroy it if he can find a value for it outside of the country.

My hon. friend must have lost his vision or else he lives in a strange part of the country, because I appeal to any farmer in this House if it is not the rarest thing possible to find mustard in a meadow of alsike, red clover, or timothy. Occasionally it may occur but it is very rare. It does not follow that the land is not saturated with the seed of these weeds that may

lie in the soil for years and years, but it does not come up until the ground is disturbed. The strange thing about it is that this seed seldom appears in a meadow. My hon. friend has had a strange experience if he has seen meadows in this country polluted with the foul weeds to which he refers. I do not agree with the hon. gentleman for King's (Mr. Fowler) that the farmers can readily comply with the provisions of section 4. I would have no hesitation in accepting the hon. gentleman's opinion on a question of law, but he will excuse me I hope if I hesitate to accept his opinion on a question affecting the farmers of this country. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) has no experience in the matter, but I can tell him that it will be practically impossible for the farmers to comply with the provisions of this Bill which require him to have his initials and surname in full upon the receptacle of every bushel of seed he sells to his neighbour.
Can't he write.
I would not cast suoh a reflection as my hon. friend does upon the farmers of this country.
It is you who have east a reflection on them.

Not at all. 1 am simply pointing out that it is highly inconvenient and that it is absolutely unnecessary. I say that it is impossible also for the farmer to have the designation of every grade of seed stamped. A farmer would have to be supplied with quite a number of appliances before he could sell a bushel of clover or , timothy to his neighbour. The minister must see how inconvenient this would be and I am sure he will modify it. I have no objection to pass stringent measures with regard to seed dealers who have all the appliances at hand, but I do think that it would be unnecessary and useless to impose such conditions on farmers who sell or exchange thousands and thousands of bushels of seeds between themselves.

The argument of the hon. gentleman is a strong reason why the Bill should be allowed to remain as it is. If thousands and thousands of bushels of seeds are exchanged or sold between farmers, it means that thousands and thousands of acres of land are exposed to be fouled by bad seeds. If it were only an occasional thing it might be overlooked, but if it is such an extensive practice as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) makes out, then the provisions of the Bill should be enforced. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) thinks that it would be a great task for the farmer to put his name upon the receptacle containing the seed, but I believe that the farmers of Canada are so well educated that they would have no difficulty in doing that. I am surprised that my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) who poses as a farmer in this
House should cast such a slur upon the farmers of Canada. It would be a long time before I would do that sort of thing. I do not think the hon. gentleman weighed well his words when he made use of them. With regard to the name of the seed, surely the farmer would know the kind of seed he was selling, having its name and grade on the bag. He would be a strange sort of farmer if he did not know whether the seed he was selling was good seed or poor seed. I do not see any difficulty in the matter. It is so simple to me that I am surprised that the hon. gentleman should take the exception to it that he does. I think I am about as much a farmer as the hon. member for Bothwell. I understand that he lives in a town and has a farm in the country. I am pretty much in the same position. I think I have as much knowledge of farming as he has, and I trust that the minister will not be influenced by the statements of the hon. member for Bothwell, but will leave the Bill just as it is.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As the discussion is entirely on the fourth section of the Bill, I think it would be better for the committee to carry the third section, and then the discussion- will be in order.
The two sections are so intimately connected that they cannot be discussed very well apart.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If it is the will of the committee, we will discuss the two together and pass the two together.

This Bill is in the right direction, and if it can be complied with, will be a great boon to the country. The farmer can comply with the law in this way. He can see before he cuts his crop, whether there is foul seed in it or not. He can tell better when it is growing than he can after it is threshed. In the latter case the seedsman is the only person who has the proper machinery to test the seeds. I believe the firm of the hon. member for Hamilton for the past thirty-five years have been the foremost seedsmen in the land, and have always had the name of selling the purest seeds, and I think he should be consulted in this matter. I am sorry he is not present, and I think the hon. minister would do well to let the Bill stand until the hon. member for Hamilton can be present. I do not think a merchant or a lawyer can tell how these seeds can be cleaned. It is a question that lies between such a man as the hon. member for Hamilton and the farmer. Even the minister himself could not decide the matter as well as these two combined.

1 quite agree with the hon. member for East Middlesex (Mr. Gilmour). I would not presume to give an opinion such as the hon. member for Hamilton could give on this

question, and it is only because X have had the advantage of expert knowledge at my disposal as a minister that I am able to take part in the discussion as intelligently as I have been trying to do. One or two points have been brought out which I would like to refer to. It is true that a great many of the dealers are not experts, and the farmers cannot be expected to be. But they can see their fields, and the object of section 3 is largely to cause the dealers absolutely to refuse to buy seeds from farmers who have had these weeds in their fields. Some of these seeds even an expert dealer with the best machinery would find it very difficult indeed to remove from timothy or clover seeds. But with this clause in operation, I believe, the seed dealers will refuse to buy from farmers who have these weeds in their land ; and that is the chief objection I have to the amendment of my hon. friend from South Ontario (Mr. Ross), who proposes to introduce into this clause words which would confine its operation to the trade in Canada. If we can cause the seed dealers to refuse to buy from the farmers who have these weeds in their land, we shall take the best step I believe towards purifying the seeds sold in the ordinary commerce of the country. If the dealers are allowed to buy these seeds for export, they will still continue to buy them from farmers who have foul land; and though they may not sell them in Canada, we will to a great extent be deprived of the benefit of this clause. When we come to clause 4, I shall be disposed to modify that so that its provisions shall not apply to the export trade, but I think it is very important that clause 3 should apply to all the trade in the country including the export trade. My hon. friend from Bothwell spoke a few minutes ago with regard to a farmer selling seed for food and not knowing what it was used for after he sold it. If a farmer sold a hundred or a tnousand bushels of oats to a grain dealer for ordinary food purposes, and not for seed purposes, he would not be responsible. If a merchant chooses to clean a supply of oats and then marked and sold, them wrongfully under section 3 of this Act, he would be responsible. Section 6 covers the sale by the farmer, not only for the purposes of food, but also to a dealer to be recleaned and sold for seed purposes. In such cases the farmer is not responsible.
What about section 4 ?

If one farmer buys seed from another, the seller can easily be relieved from the necessity of complying with this Bill by making a special agreement, and if he chooses to sell without making any such agreement he ought to be responsible for the quality of his seed just as the merchant is.

But according to section 4, the farmer would be responsible even if Hon. Mr. FISHER.
he sold pure seed, unless each sack or bag was marked as indicated in this clause. The hon. minister has pointed out this section only refers to grass seed, but it is in such seeds that the foul seeds are most difficult to discern. Under this section a farmer could not go to his neighbour and buy a bushel of clover seed and take it home and sow it, without subjecting his neighbour to the penalties therein provided. The hon. gentleman knows that two farmers would not sit down and write a special agreement absolving the seller.

The hon. member for Middlesex (Mr. Gil-mour) spoke about dealers not being experts. I am glad to say that we have been able in our city laboratory to provide machinery by which any dealer may reasonably be expected to become an expert. AVe have taken steps to provide specimens of all these weed seeds mentioned in this Bill, so that the seed merchants can get these specimens at a trifling cost and be able, with the *aid of a magnifying glass and an ordinary sheet of paper, to examine their seeds and recognize the weeds very clearly. We also have instructions prepared, which may be had for the asking, so that the merchants may without difficulty test seeds for their germinating power.

One fault found with this Bill is that it would prevent one farmer from selling to his neighbour. It seems to me there need be no difficulty about that. Suppose a farmer wants to buy from his neighbour. The neighbour says :	You understand what the law is ; if I sell you this [DOT] grain for seed I shall be responsible unless my bags are marked with my initials and the grade :	I will not sell you this grain
for seed, but if you want to buy four or five bushels I will sell it to you. So the man can buy it and do what he likes with it. He gets seed that he knows to be good, and is perfectly satisfied. I cannot see any difficulty as to this branch of the subject at all. As a dealer in seeds for thirty-two years I regard this as one of the most important measure's for our farmers ever introduced in this Dominion parliament. If there is one thing witli which we have had more trouble than any other it is with the selling of clover and timothy seed. The farmers in our section are anxious to use clover. They sow it with every crop, in order that, after the grain crop is harvested, they may let it grow and then turn it over in the fall to enrich the soil. This seeding of clover is one of the most important features of their farming, but the difficulty is in getting foul seed, particularly mustard seed. As the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) says, it is rare to find mustard seed growing in timothy, yet, as he says, that seed will remain in the ground for ten, fifteen, or perhaps as much as twenty

years, and yet germinate when yon turn up the soil. Farmers will give almost any price if they can be sure ol: getting good seed, seed that is perfectly pure and clean. Therefore, I think this Bill is in the right direction. As to exporting foul seed, I cannot agree with my hon. friend from Ontario (Mr. Boss). We should be obliged to export good seed, just as we export good butter or cheese. We want to have a reputation for first-class seed. I suppose there are a number of dealers here to-night, and I would appeal to them if it is not true that when we are buying seeds, say mangel seeds, the traveller will tell us the name of the grower in Belgium or France. We know the names of the best growers. They have a reputation, and that reputation sells their seeds. Why should we not have a reputation in the old country for our seeds, just as some of these European growers have a reputation in this country ? Certainly we should do all in our power to prevent foul seed being exported and sold as coming from this country.
Mr. SPROuLE. It is impossible it this Bill becomes law but that many farmers will violate that law". It is the custom for farmers everywhere to sell seed. They grow It and sell it for seed, because they get a few cents a bushel more profit. In my county a large number of farmers sell seed to farmers, but as well many sell it to seedsmen. This provides that the farmer shall not ' offer, expose or have in his possession for sale for the purpose of seeding ' any of these seeds, except as provided in this Bill. It will be impossible to carry out this law without many farmers coming under its penalties. They will regard it as a very great hardship. I admit the desirability of trying to prevent the use of seed containing an admixture of the seeds of noxious weeds. The minister said liis aim was to have seedsmen not buy seeds from farmers who have dirty seed. If farmers who have dirty seed are prevented from selling, nine-tenths of them will suffer. Not one case in ten, or perhaps, even in twenty, if they sold for seed, but would come under the penalties of this Act. If you carry out the law, you stop the only market the farmers have. You compel them then to sell to the seedsmen only. Nobody could purchase except for the purpose of exportation. The Bill provides that No. 1 grade of seed must have 90 per cent of germinable seed. The hon. minister says that they have a system at the Experimental Farm, which any farmer could learn, to test the germinating power of the seed. Farmers will not go into that very much. I have heard this talked up at farmers' institutes, and so on
I was referring to seed merchants when I spoke of that.

How can the farmers designate the seeds under these regulations,
as grading No. 1, No. 2 or No. 3, when many of them do not know these weed seeds when they see them ? I happen to have my office in a drug store where they buy seed year after year. And when a farmer is told that there are certain weed seeds in the seed he is selling, he is as likely as not to say :
' What are they like ; I do not know them ? ' Then the seed is spread out ori a paper on the counter and the weed seeds shown to him. These men are innocent as to violating the law, because they do not know the appearance of many of these minor seeds. It may be said that they could furnish themselves with a glass. I do not know that every farmer will do that. But even with that, he could not test how much of his seed is germinable seed. I notice the minister has not included turnip seed under this Bill. I find of late years a good deal of the wild mustard that is distributed amongst farmers is distributed in turnip seed. Almost every year where "turnips are growing we find wild mustard growing in the field. I have looked at it, but I frankly confess that I am not sure that I can tell at a glance the difference between mustard and some other seeds. If the farmer finds that what he lias bought for turnip or grass seed is full of ox-eye daisies, and he desires to enter an action against the seedsman for damages, could he, provided that law7 passes, sustain that action. Under this law, if there is more than the designated percentage of weed seeds, I venture to say, as a layman, that the seedsman would not be liable for damages to the purchaser. He wrnuld be liable only to the penalties of the law, but not for damages as w7ell. I see this young man shaking his head at it ; I do not know what significance there is in that. I do not know what his experience may be in seeds, or his legal knowledge, that would justify dissent from my statement. But I Venture to say that there are lawyers in this House who will hold that the seedsman would not be liable to an action for damages in the event of his selling seeds after this law was passed, even though there was no specific contract entered into guaranteeing that these goods were absolutely pure.

It would be a difficult thing, in fact almost impossible, to tell mustard from turnip seed, especially in some varieties. But in clause 12 the samples of this seed are to be taken within seven days of the sale, therefore, suppose a man sells his seed two or three months before it is required for sale, if it is out of his possession for seven days, according to that clause he is not responsible, and the man in whose possession it is found is responsible. This is a matter, however, that w7e can discuss later on. Now, with regard to the inspection of seeds. We have an inspection of grain, and I may safely say there is no grain, especially in this country, that it is not graded when inspected for export. It is graded No. 1, No. 2. No. 3. It is

very seldom they will take rejected grain, the grain is all graded. You notice how Manitoba grades come down, No. 1 hard, No. 2 hard, No. 1 northern, No. 2 northern, and so oh down the list. But if some of that grain happens to be frosted they will call it No. 1 frosted, or No. 2 frosted, because it will have some frosted wheat in it. Grain is inspected that way, and I think the seed law can be worked out in the same way. It is no more hardship for the farmer or the dealer to have his grain inspected, than it is for the dealer to have his seed inspected. Now, there are two places in which the dealer can sell his goods. In the first place he has the home market, and in the next place he haS the export market, and those who are in the trade know that the export market is by far the largest market for Canada. It is a trade worth looking after. Tens of thousands of bushels of clover seed are shipped out of this country. It is frequently bought in the United States, and is shipped out. It is a superior quality to that which is grown anywhere on this continent.
Who is it that buys for export ? Is it not the seedsman, who sells to the farmers again ?

Yes, but it often happens that the Ontario crop is a superior quality, superior to the crop in Wisconsin, or Indiana, or some of those states. The large market in the States for seeds is Toledo, and the merchants will probably export our prime Canadian clover seed and alsike, and they may be able to bring in American clover to take its place, because they have to pay the farmer a larger price for the Canadian seed. Under these circumstances you can see that the export market is a very large market in Canada. I cannot agree with the hon. member for Renfrew (Mr. Wright) that there would be any injustice in allowing the rejected seed to be exported. What are you going to do with these cleanings that come out of this seed V The seed must be cleaned up to a certain standard. The seedsman makes perhaps three, or four, or five grades of alsike, he will have a name for each grade.
Are there as many grades us that ?

Yes, as high as six grades of alsike. Alsike is a variable crop. One year when the crop is poor I have seen myself eight or ten different samples, no two of them alike, every grade different from the others. An exporter sends these samples home to the old country or to German}', and he sells upon these samples. Now, in cleaning these samples he has a lot of stuff that comes out and is rejected. That is known as an inferior seed. People in other countries, if they choose to buy this seed, know what they are buying, it does not ruin the reputation of Canadian seed because a good deal of our best seed has Mr. ROSS (Ontario).
been shipped every year, and still they may want this refuse seed, which is worth anywhere from one to three cents a pound. Why not let that trade go on ? It is not going to ruin our grain trade, because they know that we grow good seeds here. I cannot see why that seed should be burned up or destroyed, or that the seedsmen should not be allowed to sell it in a foreign country. I would say, don't let it be sold in Canada, because there is a trade beyond Canada, and if the foreign trade is stopped because the seed is bad, then the alternative would be to destroy the seed or burn it up. Under these circumstances I think my proposition to insert ' sale of these seeds within the Dominion of Canada ' is a proper one. I would ask the minister if he has found any vegetables in weeds which are injurious, otherwise than turnip seed, which might contain mustard ?

The Minister of Agriculture is to be congratulated in introducing this Bill. If he will make this Bill workable and succeed in eradicating foul seeds from this country so that our fields will grow nothing but what is sown on them, he will double the value of our farms. I am satisfied that the foul weeds grown in this country compose more than half of our crops. Though the minister may not be able to accomplish that much, still he is taking a step in the right direction. But we want to make this Bill so that it will not be obnoxious to the farmers and to people who raise seeds in this country. Now this section 4 says distinctly that the farmer must have his Christian name and surname on the bag of grain that he exposes for sale. Well, the farmers can all read and write, there is no doubt about that, but they have not all got bags with their names on. Again, farmers oftentimes sell to each other. Farmers that live miles from a town, or miles from a seedsman, often sell to each other. Any farmer who has a farm with a reputation for being a clean farm, and has no foul weeds in it, or none to speak of, can always sell his seed at home, whether it be seed wheat, or barley, or oats, or anything else. The neighbours all round go there to purchase seed on the farm's reputation. Consequently he has no trouble to get rid of his crop. But if there should be a few foul seeds in that grain, he is under a penalty if he sells it, unless he takes it to a seedsman. It will amount to this, that we shall have to establish seedsmen in every township. We will have to take our grain and our seeds of all kinds to them, before we can dispose of it, and have it run through mills in order to decide the question whether it is clean. I invariably run my seed wheat two or three times through a fanning mill in order to get it perfectly clean. There is some grain that it is impossible to clean thoroughly from foul seed. So if there is one foul seed in the grain-I do not see any margin left, it must all be pure

and clean-the farmer is responsible. But it is utterly impossible to take every foul seed out of a bag of clover or timothy or anything else. I remember one time purchasing a very choice variety of wheat from a seedsman in Toronto. He wrote and asked me if I would let him have the wheat that I produced from that seed. I told him I would do so, but when I threshed that wheat I found that there were some wild pea seeds in it. As I had told him I would let him have the seed I felt bound to do so. Myself and my boys went down on our knees and picked out every wild pea there was in that twenty bushels of wheat so particular was I in regard to my reputation for selling seed containing no foul seeds. Unfortunately many of us are not so particular and we must have a strict law to eradicate noxious weeds from our fields. I want to protect the farmer in this matter. The farmer generally looks out for himself, but I want to make sure that he is not made the victim of the seedsman. As I said before, and as the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has stated, oftentimes they are not seedsmen proper who purchase the seed but druggists and men who deal in all kinds of produce in the villages and towns. They have no facilities for cleaning it up. If the passage of this Bill will induce some men in each township to get screens that Will properly take out every foul seed and compel the farmers to take their seed to that man before sowing it and get it thoroughly cleaned the farmers will be, well paid for going there. Although I would like to see the Bill passed I would like to have it amended so as to be made workable. I think it will do a great deal of good in this country if it will' result in improving the quality of our seeds.

I think the Bill has a good object in view, and I am inclined to support it. I happen to know something of land where there are a lot of noxious weeds and the result is that there are some farms that are not worth $20 or $30 while neighbouring farms are worth three or four times that amount and these neighbouring farms will be worth six times that if it were not for these farms adjoining being filled with these noxious weeds. Something must be done to eradicate them, and I do not see any way of doing it except by legislation. It is fl strange thing to note that when legislation is introduced in the interests of the farmer it is sure to meet with opposition on the ground that it is against the farmer. There is a certain hardship in it no doubt, but I think it is a very reasonable provision. I do not think any farmer should be justified in doing wrong. He should not pass bad money because the law is against him and he should not sell bad seed for the same reason. I think if he sells bad seed he should be made amenable to the law the same as any other person.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) forgets that he is under penalty whether he sells bad seed or not.

The farmers should not enjoy a preferred position any more than anybody else. What we want is a law that will in some measure stop the sin'ead of these foul seeds and the depreciation in value, of farms all over the country, and if we can have a reasonable law that does not involve too much hardship it would be a very good thing, and I would like to see it go through the House. It is in the, interest of the farmers. Progress is being made in regard to farming which is largely due to legislation on the part of the various bodies in the direction of improving farming. We are doing something in this country and we have done something in the way of improving agriculture. We have succeeded in accomplishing a good deal, but yet, whenever a proposition is put forward to improve the position of the farmer the objection is taken that some how it is going to work to the injury of the farmer. It is for the farmer's good. It may work some injury but if there is a law for the general good the farmers should be made subject to that law the same as other people.

Mr. Chairman, I am thoroughly in accord with the purpose of this Bill. There.seem to be difficulties in the way of it being workable. A good deal has been said about farmers and farmers interests being protected. It may not be generally known how the large bulk of seeds of the country are marketed. The large bulk of the seeds are sold to small dealers throughout the country, some engaged in other businesses, such as the drug business, who buy direct from the farmers. Many of these men buy from and sell again to the farmers and thousands of these men who are now in business would probably be_ put out of business by the operation of this Bill as it stands at present. There would be very few instances in which the men engaged in this business would be found to be seed experts or analysts, Yet, by the operation of this Bill a man buying seed of a farmer and believing it to be pure, might be liable to incur the penalties of this Bill if upon a sample being drawn and sent to a seed analyst it were found to contain weed seeds. Provision is made for the grading of seed. Who is to grade it ? Who is to say whether seed is No. 1, No. 2, or No. 3 ? I just throw these observations out to show some of the difficulties that are in the way. I would suppose that facilities should be provided by the experimental farm so that every one engaged in dealing in seeds could gain as accurate a knowledge as possible of the character of weed seeds that are found more particularly in turnip and clover seeds. I obtained a number of samples myself for one person engaged in this business. But, you would need to do

648S
more than this; you would need to provide some practical Instruction in order that the dealer might be able to test samples of seeds submitted to him for sale. Without some provision of this kind the operation of the Bill would lead to great difficulties all over the country. The result of which would be that people engaged in this business would practically be put out of business. I would not throw any obstacle in the way of making it a practicable measure as far as possible, but a thorough ventilation of it in all its phases, ought to be made in the committee.

GIRARD (Chicoutimi and Saguenay) (Translation.) Mr. Chairman, the Bill now under discussion is the most important that has ever been submitted to parliament in the interest of the farmers. It is a well known fact in the province of Quebec and throughout Canada, that the worst evil farmers have to contend with is the spread of weed seeds. They come on us unawares, spread like wildfire, and attempts to eradicate them, which generally end in failure, require a heavy expenditure.
As stated by the hon. Minister of Agriculture, for a long time past, farmers' clubs and farmers generally have urged on our public men the need of a law which would enable them to put a stop to the spread of weed seeds. I have much pleasure in congratulating the hon. minister on having prepared a Bill which seems to me to cover pretty well the whole ground, and which, I expect, will have the desired result. However, the Bill should not deal merely with weed seeds ; it should deal also with the germinating power of seed grain. It is contended that this Bill goes a little too far. To my mind, weed seeds are not any better than poisonous substances. The law regulating the sale of these substances by druggists is very strict; however, its need for the protection of the public is generally admitted. I cannot see why we should not have a law just as strict to prevent growers and sellers of noxious seeds from palming them on tire community, for they are poison to the land, and the land is tne source of all agricultural wealth. It is most important that the latter should be provided with the best seeds available, since efforts to convince them of the desirability of growing their own grain and grass seeds have failed.
It has also been contended that this Bill will impose on the farmer conditions, as mentioned in the various sections, which he cannot comply with, besides entailing heavy expenses. The farmer sees his crops growing ; he is in a position to judge of the quality of the grain. Therefore he is at fault if he does not instruct the buyer as to the quality of the product; and for the same reason later on, the wholesale or retail dealer will offer for sale inferior seeds, without advising the buyer. Should the proposed Bill do away with the neglectful Mr. RICHARDSON. ,
habits, to say the least, of many of our farmers and seedsmen, that would be, to my mind a good reason for carrying it through. These neglectful habits have become too general ; we should endeavour to correct them, if possible; and consequently I think, the provisions of the Bill should apply to producers as well as to sellers of poor seeds. Under the provisions of the Bill, both the farmer and the dealer are compelled to have their seeds inspected before putting them on the market ; or else they have to advise the buyer of the facts. Otherwise, they are liable to pay heavy fines, which is only fair, to my mind.
It has also been stated that under the provisions of this Bill, seedsmen will be liable to heavy penalties on account of the many requirements which are therein laid down. I know of farmers and farmers' clubs who have purchased seed grain grown in other parts of the country specially with a view to improving their crops, and these seeds failed to germinate, 'the result being a total loss for the too confident buyer. And the dealer would allege that he acted in good faith, that he had not guaranteed anything, and would leave the farmer suffer the whole loss. Is that fair, Mr. Chairman, should not the seller be held responsible under such circumstances ? By providing that the producer and seller shall guarantee the germinating power of the seeds they supply and making them liable for any losses inflicted on 'the buyer through these inferior seeds, we shall be protecting farmers to a great extent against a ruinous evil.
I am a farmer myself ; I have the honour to represent a newly settled and rapidly developing district. Its virgin lands certainly do not contain any foul seeds ; and nevertheless, we are already obliged to wage war on weeds, which spread rapidly, as we are buying from outside, large quantities of agricultural seeds. I am glad to acknowledge that generally Canadian seeds are not as foul as others ; but a large proportion, all the same, is not absolutely pure.
Once more I congratulate the hon. Minister of Agriculture on having had the good sense and courage to introduce this Bill, heedless of unpopularity (should unpopularity attach to it); for his intention is, by means of a judicious and strict law to protect to the utmost limit possible the great farming interests of the country.

I may say that I have had the pleasure of meeting some of the electors of my hon. friend (Mr. Girard) in the district of Lake St. John and Chicoutimi, and amongst the requests in favour of a Bill of this kind, has come most urgently a request from his county. There the people are cultivating land, which is comparatively speaking, new, in a district of extreme richness and fertility and great possibilities for agricultural de-

velopment, and where fortunately up to the present time they are not troubled with weeds as we In the older parts of Canada are. I can appreciate well their extreme desire to be protected from the introduction of the bad weeds whiok the older parts of Canada are suffering from to such an extent. There are one or two points in the discussion which it would be as well to clear up as there seems to be a misconception about them. Section 3 which is under discussion is applicable to all cereals, grasses, clovers forage plants or vegetables. That includes certain very bad weeds which have been picked out by the experts as being the weeds that no seed sold in Canada ought to contain for whatever purpose they are sold. Section 4 deals with only the seeds of timothy, red clover and alsike and does not apply to the seeds of ordinary cereals. A good deal of the discussion bas turned on the farmers sale of large seeds, meaning the ordinary grain seeds. Section 4 does not apply to that, and consequently the farmers can carry on that trade without being liable to the penalties under the Act. Section 4, however, does apply to the farmer who sells his neighbour red clover, alsike or timothy, and he is obliged to put his name upon the package and the name of the seed and the grade. My hon. friend from Bothwell said that even if the farmer sold a practically pure seed he was liable to the penalty. He is only liable if he refuses to write his name or put the name of the seed on the package. If he puts the grade on he declares what kind of seed it is and he will not be liable to the penalty. Surely it is not too much to ask the farmer when he has to put his name on it to state the kind of seed, and if he is selling pure seed to put the grade on it. I cannot consider that this would be any hardship. If he is selling his seed to his neighbour which does contain adulterated seed he ought to be liable to the penalty just as anybody else who undertakes to sell such seeds. I am not prepared to advocate that the farmer should be free from the responsibility which he himself expects should attach to another person when the course of trade is reversed.
Who would be better able than the farmer himself who grows the seed to judge whether it is pure or not?

Yes, and if he knows that his field is- free from weeds he can say that his seed is free from weeds. I do not think any person would complain of the farmer being liable to the penalty under the circumstances.
Many farmers who have grown grain all their lives are not able to draw the distinction which would enable them to grade it. It is only an expert who can do that.
We have provided ourselves with the necessary machinery for properly grading seeds, and if a farmer chooses to send his samples of seed to the laboratory we can tell him what it contains.

Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that before a farmer could sell a bushel of clover seed to his nearest neighbour, he would be compelled to send it down here to have a report made upon it ? If that is the case, let me tell the hon. gentleman that it is absolute nonsense.

The hon. gentleman may choose to say so. If the farmer wants to sell his seed as No.
1 quality, he can sell it as such by sending a sample of it and getting it graded as No. ]. If he thinks he is not safe in selling it as No. 1, he can grade it as No. 2. I confess that I have not yet seen an amendment to this clause which would accomplish what my hon. friend wishes, and at the same time retain the efficiency of the Act ; nor have I been able to draw up such an amendment. If the hon. gentleman will draw up a clause which will do so, I shall be glad to accept it. The explanation which I have given will show how the farmer can protect himself if he wants to enter into this kind of trade. The hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Richardson) spoke a few minutes ago of the very large proportion of seeds sold in that way between farmers. I venture to say, so far as grass seeds, clover, alsike and timothy are concerned, that except for a small portion of western Ontario, the great bulk of these seeds pass through the hands of the wholesale seed dealers all over Canada.

I am endeavouring to make the Bill as perfect as possible without being harassing, and I think the hon. gentleman has found the solution of the difficulty I am pointing out. The hon. gentleman is quite right in saying that in only a small portion of the whole Dominion of Canada is the seed sold other than through wholesale dealers. If that be the case, why not confine the Bill to the seed dealers, who compose 99 per cent of those who are dealing with seed, and exempt the farmers from these regulations which it is impossible for them to fulfil, seeing that only a small section of them would be affected ?

The hon. gentleman suggests that as a compromise, which is worthy of consideration, although I fear that the farmers in that part of the country who want to buy seeds from their neighbours would not be altogether satisfied with the proposal. However, as I said at the beginning of the discussion. that I wanted suggestions, and as I do not wish to lay myself open to the accusation of being unduly set in my opinion, I am quite willing to take that suggestion

into consideration. It will, however, come into section 4, and when we come to that section, we can let it stand, to see if any such amendment can he worked out with safety.

I would ask the minister ^that he thinks of striking out the word ' vegetables ' ? In reading section 4, I am at a loss as to what is the true meaning of the Act. It is a question in my mind whether it is the package, the sack, or the bag from which the seed is sold that must be stamped, or whether it is the receptacle into which the merchant puts the seed for the farmer to take it away ? If it is the latter, it would involve such an enormous amount of work as to make it almost impracticable. If the grade of the seed and the name of the seller had to be stamped on all these little flve-cent packages of cabbage seed, onion seed and other small garden seed.
My hon. friend will find that the word ' vegetables ' does not occur in section 4, which requires the marking on the package. It occurs in section 3 only.
Well, what about striking out the word ' vegetables ' 1

I understand that the word ' vegetables ' is required for the purpose of covering the seeds of roots which are used for farm purposes, such as turnips, mangolds, carrots, and rape. In mangold seeds, I believe that wild oats not infrequently occur. Of course, it may be said that in the root crops, where tlie land is thoroughly hoed, the destruction of weeds is not very difficult, and if the word ' vegetables ' were struck out, it would not interfere seriously with the aim of the Bill. At the same time, it was thought well to include that word and make the Bill applicable to these root crops so far as section 3 is concerned.
I suppose the minister is aware that some seeds will not grow after they are two years old. Has he made any provision for them ?
The grading show's. Grade No. 1 requires therefore, that there should be 90 per cent of good growing seeds in the sample sold.

How is it possible for the purchaser to know old seed from new ? There are some seeds, such as parsnips, which will not grow the second year. It would be as injurious to the farmer to sow a crop and not have it come up as to sow foul seed.
If a seedsman sells seeds which will not grow, he certainly is injuring the purchaser. The dealer and the purchaser can always test the seed. If a purchaser buys seed and has

any suspicion of it, he can send a sample to the laboratory here and have it tested for germination just as well as for weeds. Or he may test it himself. It is a simple thing to take 100 or 200 seeds and germinate them in a piece of blotting paper moistened at a certain temperature. In a day or two, or a week or twro, according to the seed he is testing, he will see what percentage are good. If he then wishes to take out a prosecution, his safest way is to send samples of seed to the laboratory, because the report of the laboratory will be conclusive proof. But he can test the seeds at home, and then swear what percentage was not germinable.

But usually the purchaser of the seeds has not time to germinate them. He wants to put them in the ground as soon as he gets them. I think that the seller ought to be responsible for the growing. I heard the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Ross), a few moments ago, describing the different grade of seeds growing in his county-1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th. 5th and 6th of one particular seed. He said that grade 6 was such inferior stuff that there was no difficulty in shipping it to Europe and finding a sale for it. But, for heaven's sake, make a law to prevent such seeds being sold in England, because that will give a bad name to all Canadian seed.

I think my hon. friend from Elgin (Mr. Robinson) misunderstood me. When the alsike crop is harvested and threshed, you will find sometimes a dozen samples entirely different. Of course, you could mix them up and make one sample, or you could make several samples. They would all have some measure of goodness, but some of them might have what is called ungerminable seed.
