It is only when the crop is uneven, when the season has been bad, that that sort of thing would occur. It does not always follow that because seed does not grow the seedsman or the seller is at fault. No one can guarantee seed to grow. If the weather, soil, and other conditions are right, the seed will germinate if good ; but if the proper conditions are not present, that seed will not germinate, or only a very small proportion. That is particularly true of garden seed. I was going to ask the hon. minster whether the term ' vegetable ' included garden seeds which are sold in small quantities, such as lettuce, cress and cabbage seeds ?
Yes.

Because they are largely sold in packages ; and although seed-men collect them every year, there are sometimes complaints from the customers that they did not think the seed was good, because it did not come up. But that does not always follow. If you have not the conditions of weather, soil, &c., you will not get good results.

(Translation). Mr. Chairman, with the indulgence of the House, I wish to join with the hon. member for Chicoutimi and Saguenay (Mr. Girard) in congratulating the lion. Minister of Agriculture on having introduced the Bill now before us. I think it will have a most decisive effect in checking the spread of weed seeds ; it would be wasting time to urge this point any further. However, X shall venture to suggest an amendment for the hon. minister's consideration, which would render it more effective. Its effect would be to protect certain parts at least of the province of Quebec against frauds inflicted on its farmers and which the latter, to my knowledge, are unable to detect beforehand. I refer to the sale of grain for seed which is not suitable for that purpose. It is to my knowledge that in the counties of Charlevoix and Chicoutimi and Saguenay, some years ago, a considerable quantity of rye was sold as spring rye, while it was an autumn variety. I know of farmers who after having sown, ten, fifteen and twenty bushels of this, did not reap a bushel the next autumn and found out to their sorrow that they had completely lost their time and money.
T remember that last year a large quantity of wheat was sold for seed, and after germinating the grain did not make enough growth to give a crop. In other words, farmers "are too often deceived as to the quality of the seed grain they buy. The evil I am pointing out may be difficult to do away with ; however, I think the hon. minister, with the practical turn of mind for which he is noted, will realize the importance of my suggestion and the need for providing a remedy.
It may be objected that farmers can protect themselves by requiring a guarantee from the dealer as to the quality of the seed grain he sells. Practically, that guarantee, does not amount to much. In the first place, many farmers buy with implicit confidence and do not require any guarantee whatever. Besides, dealers have become *cautious. They are careful to have printed on their invoices the words : ' Without any guarantee.' That has occurred on several occasions to my knowledge.
Therefore, it would be desirable, to my mind, to amend the Bill in such a way as to compel the dealer to ascertain the ger-minative power of wheat, rye and other grains which he has for sale. Such a clause might be drafted so as to protect also the farmer who, having asked for seed to be used in the spring, gets instead, seed which can be used for autumn sowing only, a practice very little followed in the province of Quebec.

The point raised by the hon. member for Charlevoix is surely worthy of our most serious consideration. I shall ascertain whether it is practical to draft an amendment on the lines stated by him. I must admit frankly that this Bill does not go quite as far as I would wish, but it should not be forgotten that we must learn to walk before we can run. True, this Bill does not provide for the farmers as much protection as I would have liked. I would have preferred one more comprehensive ; but it seems to me it is about all we can do just now. I may say to my hon. friend (Mr. Angers) that I shall be glad to consider his suggestion and to comply with his request if it appears to me possible to do so.
On section 3,
speakername: The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Hon. Mr. Fisher.) (Translation).

speechtext: It seems to me that the minister ought to take into consideration the objection made to including vegetable seeds under section 3. It will be almost impossible to conduct the seed business as it has been conducted in Canada if this Bill comes into effect, so far as concerns the seeds sold in small quantities for garden use. The Bill should be confined to the seed sold for what is generally known as field culture, such as mangles, sugar beets, turnips, and rape, if necessary. But to apply this law to seeds sold in small packages would be absolutely impossible. These seeds are, for the most part, sold to the trade in very clean form. I do not think there is much adulteration. Probably the only defect would be failure to germinate a proper proportion. At the same time, they do, as a rule germinate sufficiently to satisfy all purposes of garden crops. I believe the trade is united in being opposed to the inclusion of the small garden seeds, and I think the hon. minister should give weight to their views. I suppose this Bill would include flower seeds ?
No.

If flower seeds are excluded, there would be almost equally good reason for excluding these garden seeds. The minister could frame a clause which would have the effect of restricting this Bill to seeds sold for field purposes. It would be impossible to apply it to the trade in garden seeds, after having experience of the Bill for a few years, it might be possible to put in a clause then to cover this other branch of the trade.
I do not see the need of including turnips and mangels, for they are sowed in rows, and weeds can be destroyed. The same is true of garden seeds. But it is quite different with grain or clover.

1 would protest against the exclusion of most of these that are called garden seeds. There is more wild mustard distributed in rape and turnip seed than in

any other way, because we cannot distinguish it. The Bill should apply to field vegetables at least.

In view of the objections raised, I may say that 1 have not been anxious to include ordinary vegetable seeds as sold in small packages, though I think it would be very easy for the seed merchants to have these seeds cleaned and to sell them so that they would conform to this Act. I sympathize with my bon. friend from Centre Wellington (Mr. McGowan) who wishes turnip and rape seed to be included under the Bill, for I know that a great deal of mustard is distributed in seed sold under these names. It is very hard to distinguish mustard from turnip or rape seed, and I have been told that it is even mixed with them intentionally. I would be glad to allow this section to stand with a view to preparing an amendment to cover the point raised by my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell) who desires the ordinary garden vegetable seeds not to be included.

We import practically all our mangel, turnip and carrot seeds, and these should be especially provided for, to secure their purity. Some amendment might be prepared so that we could regulate this trade in a wholesale way before the seeds were put in packages and provide how long they shall stay out for sale. I am not prepared to advise the minister in regard to that, but If the Bill is to stand, that might be taken into consideration. For instance, you sell a package of seeds for five ceiits; and, if It is'not up to the standard required by the law the penalty may be $100. That is an enormous penalty for the sale of a five-cent package of seeds. Under these circumstances, it would naturally be suggested that these seeds he exempt from the operation of the law. As to the suggestion I gave to the minister with regard to the export trade, do I understand that that trade is provided for in another section of the Bill ?
Yes. section 4.

So far as this section S is concerned, either the Act will be a dead letter, or else farmers who sell seed, as many of them do, will be liable to the penalties of the Act. The custom of buying and selling seed among farmers exists in my section of the country, and the ordinary farmer cannot say what is pure seed, nor can he grade his seed with any certainty of knowing what he is doing. He has not machinery to clean it, and, even if he had, there is no machinery that will certainly remove all these weed seeds from grass and clover seeds. The seeds are of the same size and very much the same shape, and you may screen the seed as often as you like, but you Mr. McGowan.
cannot remove all these impurities. There is an establishment within twenty feet of my office where they have been handling seeds for years, and they have as good and modern machinery for cleaning seeds as there is in this country. Yet, seeds from that source, believed to be as pure as they can be made, contain a great many of these weed seeds. The seed sold by the farmer cannot be free from these weed seeds. And no farmer selling to his neighbour will enter into contract to supply pure seed.
The farmer can sell seed to the dealer without being subject to this law.
But the dealer who buys it is often a retail dealer who sells it to the farmer without being cleaned at all, and such a dealer cannot grade the seed.

I have not made a careful examination of the Bill of the Minister of Agriculture, but I heard part of the remarks made by the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Angers), and I am afraid this Bill will greatly interfere with the farmers. We are not prepared for that kind of legislation now. It is an interference with the liberty of trade amongst the farmers, although perhaps the object of the Bill is good. For that reason I protest against this section at the present time.
On section 4,
The intention is that in any particular transaction the person who sells will be liable to the penalty if he sells what he does not represent.
Can he sell out of a bin?

He would have to sell just what was marked on the bin. The country merchant or retailer buys from the wholesaler, then the country merchant or retailer would be responsible except as I propose to provide by an amendment, where the package has been sealed and the name of the wholesaler is upon it and it is sold without the seal being broken. I propose to amend by inserting after the words ' indelible manner ' at the end of the first clause of section 4, the words ' either on the receptacle, package sack or bag itself, or on a label securely attached to said receptacle, package, sack or bag.' That allows a label to be .attached to the bag instead of the bag itself being marked. This amendment is made in view of the objections which are urged by the wholesale trade who say that when they mark a bag for export especially, the receiver in the other country objects to the marking on the bag, and wants nothing to be on it except the address. But as long as the bag remains in this country it would have the label with this mark attached to it.
Would the wholesaler be willing that this label should remain on the bag and used again ?

I propose to offer an amendment with regard to the seal. In a transaction between the retailer and the purchaser, the wholesale merchant would not be liable for the receptacle which had a seal upon it which had been broken.
Then whenever the seai is broken the second dealer is responsible ?

Yes, the only one responsible. The intention of the Act is to render the seller liable. If the retail merchant sells seeds the purchaser can attack him, but he cannot attack the wholesale dealer from wrhom the retailer has bought goods unless there is a package on which there is a seal unbroken, then the retail dealer would be free from responsibility, and the wholesale dealer would be responsible, but only when he sold a package with the unbroken seal.
Mr. MeGOWAN. Will the wholesaler be allowed to get out of any responsibility in connection with this Bill ? Because most of the wholesale seedsmen have special arrangements to protect themselves from any liability ?

I think this will neutralize any non-warranty clause by which they might try to relieve themselves from a guarantee of the purity or goodness of the seed. Under this section no such clause would be recognized. But I am not a lawyer, and must speak with diffidence. I suppose that under the common law a person can make an agreement with another party to relieve himself of responsibility. But this Bill I think will do away with any release to the wholesaler under what is called a non-warranty clause.
Mr. MeGOWAN. I am afraid it won't, unless you make special provision for it.

In the section where I live, large quantities of American timothy seed come into the country to be sold. I would like to know whether the wholesaler or retailer would be responsible for the foul seed that might be found in it ?

The retailer who sells to the farmer will be liable unless he is selling a package sealed with an unbroken seal. If he sells a package with an unbroken seal, then the wholesaler whose name is on that package would: be liable: but if the seal is broken, or if he sells it out of the package in a small quantity, then the retailer would be liable.

Does the minister consider the grades are sufficient, grade No. 1, No. 2, No. 3 ? I suppose the intention of 204
the Act is to make all seeds of uniform grades throughout the country.
As nearly as possible.

As it is now, every seed dealer in the country has a name on his package. Sometimes they designate their seeds as ' fancy,' ' choice.' Sometimes they will use the names of furbearing animals, as the ' martin,' ' ermine,' ' lynx,' ' fox.' the names of birds, the ' canary,' ' blackbird,' and so on. This is a radical departure from that particular phase of the subject, and I should like to know from the minister whether his Bill will interfere with that part of the trade ?

If the hon. gentleman reads the latter part of this section he will see that it contains this provision :
And the said mark may be accompanied by another designation or grade mark, provided that such designation or grade mark, is not inconsistent with, or marked more conspicuously than the one of the said four marks which is used on the said receptacle, package, sack or bag.
The section following defines what grade No. 1 must be, and what grade No. 2 must be, what grade No. 3 must be, and any merchant, if his grade No. 1 fulfils the conditions in section 5, can use any other mark that he chooses in addition to grade No. 1 to indicate the degree of the grade. He may say that it is superfine No. 1, or extra No. 1, or pure gold No. 1, or whatever he chooses, and he may have two or three grades of No. 1 upder the definition in section 5 of No. 1 according to his ideas of the quality of his No. 1 grade. The same would apply to No. 2 and No. 3.

The fact of the matter is that under the present practice of the seed trade, instead of there being four grades as the hon. minister points out, there will be sixteen or twenty grades of timothy seeds.
1 hardly think as many as that.

The practice of the trade is to sell fancy, choice, prime, strictly prime, and one or two lower grades. Now, every one of these would fulfil the requirements of this Bill. Fancy seed might be free from the particular weed seeds which are mentioned which must not occur in No. 1 seed and which is germinable to the extent of 90 degrees. Fancy seed, I might premise depends very largely on the appearance of the seed.
Not under this Bill.

Not under this Bill but in trade. The plumpness, the colour, the ab-



sence of shelled seed in timothy. These are the things that make the value in the estimation of the dealer. You may conceive-ably have fifteen or sixteen grades of timothy seed under the operation of this Bill and it would unquestionably lead to enormous confusion and difficulty. The merchant, might with jierfect honesty offer to a dealer in this country or abroad seed and it might yet be very inferior seed. It might only be a prime seed and only come within 50 per cent of a fancy seed and it might comply with all the conditions expressed in this Bill. So that, it is going to be perfectly impossible for merchants to handle their seeds and if it can be done it will require some long experience. However, I understand from the hon. minister that it is not likely that this Bill is to become law this year.
I would not like to say that.
It will be very important that we discuss it fully and give the trade time to express their objections to it.
By all means.

I think so, because if the Bill is made to apply beyond the wholesale dealer it will throw the trade into an awful state of confusion for one year at least, and I think the hon. minister should be careful to give the trade a year to become familiar with its provisions. This Bill should certainly not come into operation without a year's notice. In reference to the matter of marking, every package containing seeds must be identified at every stage of its progress with the name of the maker and a dis-cription of the contents on the package. If the wholesaler sells a bag of timothy or clover to the retail merchant it will go to the retail merchant with the name of the wholesaler either marked upon the package or on a tag firmly attached to the package, then a description of the kind of seed and then the designation of the grade of seed. Between the wholesaler and the retailer there very often comes the jobber who buys from the wholesaler and sells to the retailer. When it comes into the hands of a jobber the liability on the part of the wholesaler ceases after seven days. This package would require to receive a new mark. It would then be marked with the name of the jobber. There would be a tag containing the name of the jobber, the name of the seed, the description of the seed and its grade. Then, it comes into the hands of the retailer and after seven days time the retailer would have no claim against the jobber. He is the man who is going to sell it to the public, and against whom the retail buyer would have no recourse after seven days. Then, it will require to be tagged again with the name of the retailer, the name of the seed and the grade. The con-Mr. BELL.
sequence is that the package, after a short time will be covered over with marks and it will be absolutely impossible to mark the packages. Therefore it is quite clear that the adoption of a tag instead of a mark is absolutely essential because the bag will be covered with all these marks. The result of this will be that in the next season a bag which has a second hand value of fifteen or sixteen cents would practically be useless because it would have all over it the marks of the previous season and it would not be properly descriptive of the merchants name or of the contents. Unless some way of avoiding this difficulty were arrived at, the dealer would have an enormous quantity of bags which would be useless. In view of that, and in view of the fact that properly to comply with the terms of the Bill, this package will be required to be marked at every stage of its progress from the wholesaler to the jobber, then to the retailer and to the final purchaser or the customer who is going to use the seed, it is absolutely necessary that some way of getting over the difficulty of this marking should be arrived at.
My hon. friend (Mr. Bell) apparently did not hear the amendment which was proposed to obviate the difficulty in regard to that.
That is to use a tag ?
Yes.
I did hear that.
That disposes of the difficulty.
But did the hon. minister think of the difficulty this article would encounter in its progress in the trade ?
They would simply put a new tag on.

In view of the fact that there are heavy penalties in this Bill for the improper sale of seeds, what provision have you made for the retailer ? As I understand" the transaction will go through something like this :	The wholesaler will
sell to the retailer a bag of turnip seed. It will probably have on it the tag of the wholesaler. The retailer puts that bag up for sale and be sells it in quantities ranging from half a pound to five or ten pounds. Does the tag remain on the bag until it is all sold and is it to be regarded as the guarantee of the wholesaler until it is all sold, or is the wholesaler relieved of his liability after seven days and does it then come upon the retailer ?

Yes. The wholesaler will be relieved when the seal is once broken on the bag. As soon as the bag is opened, except for the taking of

a sample from it, the wholesaler would be relieved because he could not be held responsible after the bag was opened. The wholesaler does not know what the retailer may do with the seed after he once opens the package.

The more I look on section 4 the more I think it is calculated to create a great disturbance as to the relations between farmers in the country. As I understand section 4 it would be impossible for farmers to deal amongst themselves in timothy and clover seeds. Some of these farmers are known in certain parts of the country as having excellent seed for sale and if they have to comply with all the requirements of section 4 it would be a great hardship for them. I do not think this Bill is workable, and if I am in order I would move that the committee rise.

Of course the hon. gentleman is quite in order in moving that the committee rise, but I must ask the committee to reject it. I am quite willing later on to ask the committee to rise, report progress, and ask to sit again, but as this motion of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) would practically dispose of the Bill for this session I cannot agree to it. The hon. gentleman says the Bill is not workable. He was not present at the earlier part of the session when I stated that I was not absolutely committed to the details of the Bill, and that I was quite prepared to receive suggestions, and if the Bill could be made more workable by these suggestions to adopt them. I do venture to think that the Bill is workable even in the form in which it stands. The objection which the hon. gentleman takes to this particular section has been discussed for some time, and so far I have not been convinced of the difficulties that my hon. friend points out. It is true that if a farmer sells to another farmer timothy or clover or alsike which he does not choose to mark with his own name, the name of the seed, and the grade, he will be liable to the penalties under the Act. The intention of the Bill is that the people who sell seeds shall be required to guarantee the quality of the seeds they sell. People who sell seeds shall be required in some way to guarantee them. If the farmers themselves chose to engage in the business I must confess that they should be liable to the same conditions that people who sell seeds ordinarily are obliged to live up to. I am quite willing to acknowledge that there might be an occasional case of hardship, but the instances would be very few indeed. I said to the hon. gentleman from Bothwell that if he would propose an amendment to this clause which would not interfere with the efficacy of the Act I would be very glad to consider that amendment, but so far no such amendment has been proposed, and I confess that I have not been able to work out an amendment which would ac-204*
complish that without interfering with the efficacy of the measure.

Mr. Chairman, while approving of the principle of this Bill, and realizing the pressing need of legislation of this kind for the province of Quebec and the counties generally, with a view to the improvement of our seed grain ; and while I am aware that large quanties of grain containing seeds of noxious weeds are offered for sale daily ; I must disagree with the minister in regard to clauses 3 and 4 relative to trade between farmers. To my knowledge, in the county which I have the honour to represent, there is going on among the farmers an interchange of grains, from parish to parish, much to their benefit. But, under the provisions of the Bill now before the House, farmers taking part in this trade would be apt to pay pretty heavy penalties. To my mind, that would be unfair and would result in preventing farmers from carrying on a business profitable to themselves.
Then again, it does not seem fair to me to make the retailer liable to a penalty. The hon. minister is well aware that when the retailer receives the seeds from the wholesale dealer, he does not offer them for sale in the condition in which they reach him, that is to say, in closed bags or sacks. It will therefore be necessary for him to break the seals on these bags ; and it seems to me it would be most unfair, on account of this simple act, to hold the retailer responsible for the quality of the seeds contained in the bags. I am inclined to believe that the minister, on thinking the matter over, will realize that he is doing an injustice to the retailers, especially those dealing in timothy and clover seeds, which are generally sold in small lots.
It would be unfair to hold the retail dealer responsible for the quality of the seed sold by the wholesale dealer, merely for the fact of his breaking the seals of the bags which contain these seeds. The hon. minister, I am assured, realizes that is of absolute necessity to amend this Bill in such a way as to protect the farmer who is anxious to secure good seed, and also to protect the merchant. It is important at the same time that the retail merchant be protected against the wholesale dealer, by relieving the former of any responsibility as."to the quality of the seed contained in bags which he merely opened on receiving them from the wholesale dealer.

I am happy to find that the remarks I made concerning the Bill are endorsed by the hon. member for Bagot (Mr. Marcil). By reading over the other provisions of the Bill, one will readily perceive how arbitrary they are. Section 4, for instance, states the many conditions which the farmer has to comply with if he wishes to sell seeds. Those who are fami-

liar with the habits of the farmers of the province of Quebec, and of Ontario, as well, will see at once how objectionable these provisions are. Not only would this section be very unpopular, but it would not be workable. The farmer who wished to sell a small quantity of seed, red clover seed, for instance, would have to put it in a special package and to label it with his initials, the name of the kind of seed, and also the name of one of the four grades mentioned. As every one will see, these provisions could not be worked easily. My hon. friend from Bagot and the minister himself who are acquainted with the habits of our country people know perfectly well that this law could not be worked. That is why I moved a few moments ago that the committee rise, to show our disapproval of the Bill, although, I admit, that disapproval should have been expressed at the time of the second reading. But, as I had to be away at the time, I take this opportunity of presenting the motion.

In reply to the hon. gentleman who represents Bagot, I would say that the country merchant who retails seeds which he has bought from a wholesale dealer can protect himself under the provisions of this Bill by taking a sample of the seeds when he buys them, and if that sample is up to the quality marked on the package, he is then quite safe in selling them in the same way. If he finds that it is not up to the quality which the wholesale merchant has marked upon the package, he can have recourse against the wholesale merchant. Of course, if he neglects to take such a sample and goes on and sells the seeds by retail, after he has broken the seal on the package, he cannot come back on the wholesaler ; and it would be hardly fair that he should, because the seal having been broken, the wholesale dealer would, not know whether the seed the retailer sold was that which he sold to the retailer or not. In that way the country storekeeper is quite able to protect himself from selling anything that is not what he represents it to be. In regard to the other matter, as I said to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). I am quite open to suggestions with regard to this Bill, and I am quite willing to consider the question as to how the farmers dealing with one another in the way he and other members have described can be protected from unfair and improper incidence of the provisions of this Bill. But that is quite a different thing from the committee rising and rejecting the whole Bill. As I have said with regard to other sections, I am willing to let this section stand for further consideration, with a view of seeing how the farmers can be protected in the ordinary transactions between themselves. But I must ask the committee to reject the motion made by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, and to go on and

consider the other sections of the Bill with the same open mind with which we have discussed the Bill thus far.
Mr. MAItCIL (Bagot.) (Translation). Before replying to the hon. minister, I wish to state to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier that I am not ready under the circumstances to support the motion he has just made, seeing that the hon. minister proposes to let section 4 stand for the present and to amend it in accordance with the views of the committee.
Now, to meet the objection made by the hon. minister, in reference to retail dealers, I wish to draw his attention to the fact that he possibly is not in as good a position as the merchants themselves to know exactly what is going on. It is likely enough to happen that the wholesaler, knowing that the retailer, by the mere fact of his breaking the seals, becomes responsible for the quality of the seeds, will put at the upper end of the bags, first quality grain, which will be classed No. 1, as required by law, while the middle and bottom layers will consist of seeds of third and fourth quality. Such frauds are frequent enough in the wholesale trade, and I may inform the minister that, on various occasions, country retailers have received bags of seed grain the upper layers of which were of first quality, while the lower layers were third quality.
If the practice is such to-day, it will continue in the future in spite of this law, and it would be unfair to hold the retailer responsible for the quality of the grain contained in the bags of which he broke the seals, considering that he is not in a position to find out whether that seed is oils not first quality. I trust the hon. Minister of Agriculture will think the matter over, and reach the conclusion that his Bill should be amended so as to protect the wholesale dealer and the country retailer.

It seems to me that the retail dealer, in order to free himself from the responsibility of selling against the law, must take the sample in the presence of the wholesale merchant who has sold it to him. If he does not do that, he must be held responsible for it. That would appear to me from clause 11.

I intend to propose an amendment coming after section 8 to the effect that any person who sells seeds by wholesale shall not be liable for the seeds sold after the seal has been broken, unless when the seal has been broken a sample for an official test has been taken in the presence of two witnesses. I intend to propose that amendment to protect the wholesale dealer and to give the retail dealer a chance to protect himself. In reply to the hon. member for Bagot, I may say that it is well known that there is a little

instrument, something like a pencil, which can be forced into a package of seeds, by which samples can be taken, not only from the top, but all through the bag. That little machine costs about twenty-five cents, and I do not think any country merchant will allow himself to be laid open to a charge, because he did not spend twenty-five cents to take the trouble to protect himself in that way. I appreciate, however, the necessity of protecting the retail dealers in the country just as much as the wholesale dealers who are selling to them. The provisions of the Bill, I hope, and the amendment which I am going to suggest, will cover these points, and I want to reiterate that I am only too glad to receive suggestions which remove the difficulties which necessarily gather around legislation of this kind. We have been fortunate enough on various occasions to thresh out various Bills to make them workable, and I have confidence that the intelligence and inventiveness of this committee will succeed in making this Bill as workable as we have made other Bills.

It is, I admit, late to move against the principle of the Bill, but still it is in accordance with the rules of the House to move now that the committee rise ; and as I and a great many other members of this House, who understand the wants of the rural population of the province of Quebec, disapprove of this legislation at the present time, although it may be useful at a later date, I wish to move-and I do it without any disrespect to the hon. minister-that the committee rise.

Considering that nearly every member who has spoken on the Bill has conceded that there is a necessity for some law governing the seed trade of this country, I think the Bill should be proceeded with. When we consider that in the province of Ontario alone the hay and clover prop, exclusive of seed, is worth 530,000,000, we can see how important this Bill is. Under the circumstances, I think the best thing we can do is to go over the Bill and see just how far we agree with it, and how far we cannot agree. I confess that there are some things in the Bill which I consider might be improved ; but I. for one, feel that we should go on and see what can be done in the matter.

I appeal to my hon. friends who know the wants of the province of Quebec in regard to legislation of this kind. This legislation, however we might remodel it, would not be acceptable to the population there. I appeal to these hon. gentlemen to give their opinion on the Bill, which I do not think is suitable either to the province of Quebec or to the province of Ontairio. I insist on my motion.

My hon. friend takes the responsibility of
*challenging a Bill of this kind, which he does in the interest of the farmers of Quebec, and intimates thereby that the farmers of that province object to a. Bill which is for the purpose of preventing their being sold bad seeds. The hon. gentleman is welcome to take that responsibility, and to go before the farmers of the province of Quebec with that responsibility on his shoulders. I challenge him to vote in this House in that pense. If	the	hon.	gentleman	and his
friends choose to vote for the destruction of this Bill at this time, I warn him that the farmers of the province of Quebec will hold him responsible when he goes before them.

My hon. friend does not deceive anybody	with	this talk.	I haveseen by the gestures of his friends behind him that they have been appealing to him to give up this Bill. I have seen by the gestures of	the	hon.	gentleman's friendsbehind him	that	they	have been	pressing
him to abandon his Bill. Among those I have noticed^ Mr. Speaker, himself, the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Monet) the hon. member for Yerchiires (Mr. Geoffrion) and the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Angers). The opinion so clearly expressed by the hon. member for Bagot (Mr. Marcil) coupled with the attitude of these hon. gentlemen, is proof positive that the hon. minister is endeavouring, in a very clumsy way, to get rid of his Bill. Let him stand up like a man and defend his Bill or keep his peace, instead of trying to shelve on me the responsibility of the abandonment of that Bill, which his hon. friends behind him have been urging him the whole evening to give up.

Mr. Chairman, there is a clear contradiction in the remarks made by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier. He apparently finds fault with the minister for not pressing his Bill through committee this evening. That is exactly what the minister wishes to do, while the hon. member is moving for the committee to rise and throw out the Bill entirely.
Is my hon. friend in favour of this Bill ?

Certainly. I have just risen to protest against the suggestion made bj; the hon. member that I was one of those who seemed to oppose the Bill. In the provinec of Quebec, as well as in all the other provinces which I had the pleasure to visit, weeds are present, and I am of opinion that such a law is needed to protect the farmers, especially in the newly settled districts where these noxious weeds have not yet taken a foothold. It is highly important that they should be kept out.
air. aiONK (Translation). Does my hon>
friend approve of section 4 of this Bill ?

1 think there are sections which are too strict and which should be amended. But in view of the minister's willingness to let clauses 3 and 4 stand, for the purpose of considering various amendments suggested by members from the province of Quebec who spoke this evening, I think we should be satisfied.
We shall examine the provisions of the Bill and retain whatever is good in them, but the proposal of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) is a greater evil, as it rejects the Bill as a whole. Hon. members on the other side who have spoken have approved of the principle of the Bill. Now, what remains to be done is to look into the details and make the necessary changes. But my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier, while in favour of the Bill, would do away with it by having the committee rise without reporting progress.
The object of the Bill is good and approved by all: What remains to be done is to work out the details with a sincere determination to adopt the best possible means for the eradication of weed seeds from our fields. In the field of politics noxious weeds have to be endured ; but such is not the case with the weeds on the farms.

My hon. friend from La-prairie says that hon. members on this side are in favour of the principle of the Bill. I was not present in the early part of the discussion, as I was on the Redistribution Committee, but if what my hon. friend says be the case, I am prepared to withdraw my motion. I would like, however, to know from my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture if he intends to carry the Bill through this session and to give us the amendments to those sections to which we have objected. Surely he is not afraid to tell us whether he intends to carry this Bill through with the changes for which we have been contending.

I do not know how often my hon. friend wishes me to express my intentions. I have already told the committee several times that, in my opinion, the time had arrived for the passage of a Bill of this kind, but that I was quite ready to discuss any amendments which might be suggested to improve the measure. I have said that I should be most happy to receive from the committee any suggestions towards making the Bill as perfect as possible.
Does the hon. gentleman from Jacques Cartier wish to withdraw his motion ?
Does the hon. minister refuse to give me the information which I asked in a most respectful manner as to whether he intends this Bill to become law or not ?

It does not lie with me to make it law. I am Mr. MONK.
in the hands of the committee and propose to be guided by the evident desire of the House. If the Bill can be made such as will meet the approval of the House, it will no doubt become law; but if it cannot be put into such a shape as to commend itself to the approval of the House, I shall not attempt to force it through the House.

I think what the hon. member for Jacques Cartier desired to know was whether the Bill shall become law this year. I understood the hon. minister to say that he does not intend to make it become law until July of next year.

When we were discussing section 2, my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier was not present, but I then stated that I thought the date fixed in the Bill for bringing it into operation was too early, and that I would let that clause stand so that we might change the date later on.
Does the hon. member for Jacques Cartier wish to withdraw his motion ?
In view of the declaration of the hon. minister that he intends completely changing his Bill, I beg to withdraw my motion.

I
cannot accept a withdrawal on such terms. I have not said that I propose to change the entire character of the Bill.
If the hon. minister states that he has no intention of changing his Bill, I shall persist in my motion.
Neither have I made any such statement as that. Surely my hon. friend does not wish me to state over again what I have already declared so often. Let him either put his motion or withdraw it.
I persist in my motion.

There is evidently some confusion or misunderstanding. No doubt the general opinion of the committee is that this Bill is in the right direction. If we could secure a supply of pure seeds, which has a large percentage of germination, no doubt that would be most desirable, but the difficulty is in getting a workable measure. I have urged on the hon. minister to proceed slowly so as to avoid throwing a very important trade into a state of confusion.
But the hon. gentleman's colleague does not want me to proceed at all.

I do not think that that is the intention of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier. I rather understood that the hon. minister himself once or twice suggested asking the committee to rise and he has allowed one or two clauses to stand over, so that we might not make too much pro-

gress. That is in agreement with the sense of the House, which believes the result aimed at very desirable but very difficult of accomplishing. The more we look into the matter, the more we find that a great deal of care and elaboration will be necessary before the measure can be put into such a shape that it will be a benefit to the country. It is possible to pass the measure in such a shape that it will prove a dead letter. It would be looked upon as a very harsh thing if large penalties were enforced against persons who, to a certain extent, were innocent and were proceeding to carry on this business as It has been carried on for many years past. The difficulty of bringing home an offence to any particular person, I am sure the hon. minister has already realized, would be enormous. At the same time, we cannot make any great mistake in going on to consider! the clause further. I do not anticipate that the minister will succeed in putting the Bill into such a shape as he will feel like making it an operative law in the course of the coming year. He could hardly do that at this late stage of the session. The House generally is disposed to take an interest in a Bill. Many members have taken part in the discussion and everybody has shown a desire to assist the minister and facilitate the progress of the Bill. Special attention has been paid to it by hon. members from the province of Quebec. One reason, no doubt, is that it will affect many people in that province. Timothy seed, of the best quality, we know is produced in Quebec, and many thousand bushels are marketed in Montreal every year. For my own part if the hon. minister does not desire to withdraw his Bill, if he will hold this section for further amendment, we might go through other sections without any great loss.

- I have already said I am opposed to the motion of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), and I have already said that I did not think it would be wise to bring this Bill into force this year. As I have said the time for the seed trade is practically upon us and the conditions imposed by this Bill will, I do not say revolutionize, but change in some respects this important trade. Therefore, I think it would be wise to delay. If the minister needs a precedent, I would refer him to the case of the Fruit Marks Act which was brought in one session and discussed, and it was then decided that some such law was needed. The Bill was left over until the folllowing session. That law has been beneficial and the treatment of il might be taken as a precedent in this case.

I confess I am a little puzzled by the action of the Minister of Agriculture. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier asked what seems to me a very fair question-whether the minister would insist that the Bill should go through in its present shape. The hon. minister had declared that
he had an open mind on the question, he invited fair discussion and said he was not averse to any reasonable amendments, but was entirely in the hands of the committee. My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier without uttering another sentence in view of the statements of the hon. minister, withdrew his amendment. To the surprise of everybody, the minister arose in something like a passion and declared that he would not allow the amendment to be withdrawn except on conditions laid down by himself. That seems a piece of pettishness on the part of the minister. I am in favour of any measure that will make for better conditions with regard to the subject dealt with by this Bill. But I would infinitely rather see the Bill stand over than have it pass in its present shape-and that is what the hon. minister means to insist upon, as is evident by his language in refusing to allow the hon. member for Jacques Cartier to withdraw his amendment. I will therefore vote for the amendment.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) has so completely misrepresented the position, unintentionally-
Order.

I am in order. He has so completely misrepresented what has occurred that I have to put him right:	The hon. member for
Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) came late into the discussion and not knowing what had been said began to criticise the Bill.

I did not criticise the Bill,
I criticised section 4.

Bill. That is the whole affair. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) will say frankly that he will withdraw his motion because it is an inexpedient motion, I am willing to agree to its withdrawal. But if lie is going to try to release himself from the tight place in which he finds himself by putting words in my mouth that I never uttered. I will not allow him to withdraw his motion on those conditions.

The hon. minister says that there has been practically no disagreement with the Bill. Why, several members expressed themselves as plainly as they could to the affect that the Bill would be unworkable. I said that for one, and I say it again. I would rather see the Bill defeated than passed in its present form. While I think it would be better for the farmers to have pure seed, I say that they cannot work under this Bill and carry on their operations as they carry them on today. Either the Bill must be a dead letter or the farmers will be punished for offences which they have no desire to commit. The hon. minister will not admit that he is going to change the Bill in any important particular
I did not say that.

He would not say that he would mend it seriously. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier is not-out of place in making the motion he has made, and I shall support him.
Amendment (Mr. Monk), negatived.
On section 5,

This is subject to the same difficulties pointed out with regard to section 4, as it refers to these small seeds, and I take it that it is covered also by section 6, which covers all classes of cereals and small seeds. But the hon. gentleman will see that there is no escape so far as these small seeds are concerned under section 6, because in no case are they sold for food.
Section 5 simply defined the different grades. The definition of grades is necessary.
Why do you use the word * screening ' instead of the worjl ' rejected,' to designate inferior seeds ?

I was going to ask that the word ' rejected ' be substituted for the word ' screenings,' in accordance with the suggestions of the seed dealers, who say that the word ' screenings ' is not known to the trade, while the word 'rejected' is. 1 do not think we could well refuse to allow these seeds to be sold. I am told by the trade that there is a large sale outside of Canada for these ' screenings.'
Has the hon. gentleman made some inquiry as to the uses to which these screenings are put when they are exported ?
I am informed that some poor alsike clover seed is used for dyeing purposes. I think most of these seeds are sent to the western states and used on pasture land.

I think the word 1 rejected ' will more properly meet the minister's grade because, as we understand ' screenings ' in the trade, 70 per cent of them would not germinate, and they would more properly be termed ' rejected.'
It is a grade below No. 3.
Were these tests the minister referred to carried on over a series of years ?
Over two years.

I noticed in the test for timothy that one sample in five days had seven per cent of germination, and in fourteen days the same sample had twenty-two per cent of germination. That was practically no good. Some of them were low, but most of them were high. I would ask the minister if the season in which this seed was taken was a good season for timothy seed, and was it grown in Canada or imported from the United States ? A large proportion of the timothy seed sold in Canada comes from the United States, especially that sold in Ontario, when we have a short crop. It might be that the germination for timothy seed is a little high. I see by the table he has prepared here that it runs largely from 70 per cent to 90 per cent. There would be a variation in the seasons. Timothy might be good one season and poor in another.

The tests of which I have spoken were taken in the spring of 1903, and the spring of 1902, they were tlie seeds grown the year before. They were taken both from imported and Canadian grown seed, I could not tell how- many of each, but probably more Canadian grown seed than imported. But we cannot always tell where the seeds come from. While it may be a "bad year for timothy seed in one district, it may be a good year in another district.

It is more than likely that the department germinated timothy seed which was unhulled and which was hulled. If it is timothy seed that had the rough outside coat on, then it is known as unhulled seed. Perhaps he could tell me whether there was any difference in the germinating power between non-hulled and bullied timothy seed.
Practically no great difference. As long as the seed was fresh it would germinate whether it was hulled or non-hulled.
Has the hon. gentleman an idea as to the number of officers it will be necessary to appoint in order to enforce this clause 5 ?
Any person may take action under the Act.
Where will the officers charged with the enforcement of this Act be located ?

We have no intention to appoint inspectors throughout the country. We will have only one or two officers in the laboratory here to examine the samples. Section 9 is for the purpose of authorizing them to take samples and if necessary that persons may be sent from the department at any time to enforce the Act but it is not the intention to appoint inspectors all over the country for the enforcement of the Act. The proposal is to provide machinery under the Act and let anybody take action for enforcing the penalties. In that connection the proposal is that the officers of the department shall be available for testing any samples of seed sent to them and their test will be regarded as prima facie evidence against the persons selling the seed. That is partly in the Act and partly in the regulations, which, under section IS, the Governor in Council is empowered to issue for the enforcement of the Act. I beg to move :
That the word * rejected ' be inserted instead of the word ' screenings ' in subsection 2 of section 5.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 6,
. The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE. Before adopting section 0, I wish to add a subclause. The section provides that :
The provisions contained in this Act shall not apply to
Oa) any person growing or selling seeds for the purpose of seed ; or' to
(b) any person selling seeds direct to merchants to be cleaned and graded before being offered for sale for the purpose of seeding.
It lias been pointed out to me by persons engaged in the trade that they would buy seed and hold it in their warehouses for months before they would be able to clean it and that under these circumstances if seed was not held for the purpose of sale the person holding the seed should not be liable to the penalties of the Act.

How is the farmer, or the person selling the seed, to know whether it is to be recleaned and to be sold for seeding purposes ? Paragraph (b) may be all
right but it seems to me to be rather vague.

The intention is that where a seed merchant buys seed from a farmer, if the seed has not been cleaned by the farmer and it is intended to be cleaned by the seed merchant, the farmer shall not be liable to the penalties of this Act. He could sell that seed in bulk without marking his name or putting the grade upon it, and if it were not pure he would not be liable to the penalties of this Act.

That destroys the whole effect of the section, because, if he were left perfectly free to sell it, all he would have to do would be to sell the seed and the person to whom he sold must take the responsibility of all the penalties that would follow. The person who sells does not know what disposition is to be made of it, and therefore he should not be asked to contemplate what disposition the man to whom he is selling it, is going to make of it. A difficulty is involved there and I think the person selling the seed under such conditions should be free and that the man who afterwards cleans and grades it and disposes of it for seed should be made to bear the penalties that would follow from an infraction of the law.
I think you might insert after the word ' merchants ' the words ' who are in the trade' and then hold the merchant responsible for it afterwards. The farmer could not be held responsible any longer.
It is not intended that he should be. The intent certainly is that after the farmer sells the seed to the merchant he shall not be liable to the penalties of the Act.
After he has sold it for the purpose of being cleaned and graded he cannot know whether it is to be cleaned and graded or not. After he sells it his interest ceases.
If we were to sell it to a person who was going to sell it again in the condition it was in when he sold it he should not be re-' lieved.
How would he know ?
I see what the hon. gentleman means.

Section (b) would work against the trade. I did not recognize it until now. The hon. minister explained that the farmer might sell his seed to the merchant to be cleaned and graded, but how is he going to provide for this case ? Some of the farmers clean the seeds, and I know from experience, that it is very unsatisfactory to buy uncleaned seeds from the

farmers. A farmer might not clean the seed as it would be required for sale, but be would take the dirt and chaff out, and it would then be a presentable grade. Suppose the farmer sells that seed to the merchant and the merchant does not intend to offer it for sale at his store, but intends to sell it to the wholesaler who has a cleaning apparatus and who will resell it, I think it should be made clear that they could handle that seed from the farmer to the merchant and the merchant to the wholesaler, who recleans. If the word ' or ' was added in the 37th line it might meet that case. Perhaps three-fourths of the seed that is offered to the merchant is what we would call cleaned seed, but it might not come up to the requirements of this law.
He incurs no penalty in buying, but only when he goes to sell.
In nine cases out of ten he passes the seed through a machine, and then it all comes out one grade after going through a process of mixing.

If there is any responsibility on the farmer who sells to a merchant, I would not care to have the section passed in that form. I can understand that a case of the kind mentioned by the hon. member for Ontario may arise where the retail merchant in the country was simply a go-between from the farmer to the wholesale seedman, and he perhaps ought not be subject to a penalty.

I agree with the amendment offered by the Minister of Agriculture. I think it is a wise amendment. The alsike season runs from August to November, and during the busy season it is an utter impossibility to prepare this seed for market and grade it properly.

It often occurs that a merchant may buy a carload of seed and that he will frequently turn that carload over without it being in his possession a day. It would be quite impossible for him to test the germinating quality of that seed.
I presume the merchant would buy a sample and have it tested.
It is absolutely impossible to test the sample in the busy part of the season.
If the carload of seed was not opened, the person who sold It to the merchant would would be liable.
Suppose the seller lived in the United States.
If the transaction occurred in Canada he would be liable
But many of these carloads of seed are ordered by wire.
I think the importer, when he imports from outside of the country, would have to be liable for the seed.
It might happen that the importer would have no possibility of ascertaining the germinating quality of the seed.

If we allow the importing to go on without placing any liability on the importer, it would defeat the whole object of the Bill. I have it from several men of experience that a good seedsman can tell by the eye the germinating qualities of some seeds about as well as if he had made a test. There are some seeds that you cannot tell by looking at them, but there are a great many that you can tell ; and they would know by the sample where they bought their seed. They would also very largely trust to the reputation of the people from whom they bought. If they once caught any person in that way, they would not buy from him again, and they would make it so that he could not again sell seeds in this country. If we were to receive imported seeds in the way suggested, I do not think to jail, but that is all.

How is the hon. minister going to deal with the American or English seedsmen who send seeds into this country by mail ? Sometimes they have an agent going through the country, taking orders, and the goods are delivered afterwards. The agent may not be a responsible person from whom any one could recover. Is there anything in this Bill taking care of that part of the business ?

The condition of affairs which the hon. gentleman has pointed out is somewhat familiar to me. I think the seeds sold by mail are chiefly garden and vegetable seeds; I do not think any great quantity of agricultural seeds are sold in that way. There are certain seed houses in the United States which send out considerable quantities of package seeds. It has been suggested that they should be excluded from the operation of this Act, and perhaps the fact stated by the hon. gentleman is one reason why they should be excluded. We might, however, meet that difficulty in one of two ways. The pedlar of the seeds in this country might be required to make a domicile here and be responsible for all the importations of the seeds he sold. I grant that sometimes the pedlar would not be a responsible person, and that it would be hard to get anything out of him. But sometimes they are responsible; very often they are farmers. Another way in which we might deal with the matter, if it is found to be a sufficiently prevalent practice to justify it, would be to require that seeds sold in that way should be entered at some particular port, where samples would be taken,

and where they would be liable to penalty or confiscation if not up to their grade. I confess that that is one of those difficulties which I have not quite solved in dealing with this measure.
Section allowed to stand.
On section 7,

I think the words ' hard labour ' should be struck out of this section. Suppose a man should buy ten pounds ot seeds or sell ten pounds of seeds he would be sent to jail at hard labour. I would suggest that the penalty be according to the amount of seeds sold. If a man sold a thousand pounds, it might be right enough for him to pay the penalty of $10; but if he sold ten pounds, that penalty would be severe. In our district we have no such place as hard labour; we can send a man to jail, but that is all.

This clause is taken, I think verbatim, from the General Inspection Act, and the penalties are the same as they are there. I suppose we might strike out the words ' hard labour ' if that penalty is thought to be too hard. But that portion of the clause, and also the amount of the fine running from $100 down to $10, is supposed to be left to the discretion of the magistrate who imposes the sentence.

It seems to me that It is rather an excessive penalty to make the minimum fine for each offence $10. ' If a person sold half a dozen packages of vegetable seeds, he would be liable to pay a fine of $10 for each package sold. That would impose an enormously heavy penalty for what would be a trifling injury.

I believe that fraud is the same thing, whether the amount of seed sold be large or small. 1 believe that the clahse as it reads is all right, except perhaps that it is a little too harsh for the first offence. This is a new Act, and I suppose that everybody who will come under its provisions will be guilty for the first time. Suppose a person should be prosecuted under this Act. Suppose he should be brought to a justice of the peace, who would be very severe upon him and sentence him for the whole amount of the penalty, $100. The man is unable to pay that. So he will have to be condemned to jail, with or without hard labour. If this was his first offence, I think that sentence would be found to be Very hard upon him. I would suggest that for the first offence, the accused should be dealt with very leniently, as this will be a new law and should not be too rigorously administered in the beginning. Let the justice of the peace be as severe as possible in the case of second or third offences, but not in the case of a first offence.

The hon. the minister has said that we would leave the penalty to
the discretion of the justice of the peace. I am a justice of the peace myself and I would advise the hon. minister not to trust them too much because some of them will be inclined to give too hard a dose. Justices of the peace are sometimes very crusty and will go the full length the law allows, when there is no necessity for it. Better not leave the matter entirely in their hands.
Does my hon. friend suggest that we should make a fixed penalty for each offence and leave no discretion to the magistrate ?
I would do that if I were in the hon. minister's place.

I do not think it would be right to impose a fixed penalty, because there might be differences in the guilt of the accused. At the same time the margin is rather large-from $10 to $100. Why not say from $10 to $25 or from $10 to $50.
Or reduce it to $5.

I will let that section stand.
Section allowed to stand.
The person on whose behalf any seed is sold, offered, exposed or had in possession for sale, contrary to the provisions of the foregoing sections of this Act, shall be prima facie liable for the violation of this Act.
In what case shall he not be liable ?

If he proves that it was sold by an agent not authorized or who tampered with it, without his knowledge or order, he would escape liability. But if his clerk or storeman sold it, he would be liable prima facie, and he would have to prove that his employees had acted contrary to his orders or had intentionally deceived him.
If that be the intention, far better to say so.
It does say so practically.

I should not think so. You have statutes in which a man is held liable even without any intention to violate the law and others in which the intention is necessary. I suppose section 8 is in the latter category.
It is reproduced from the General Inspection Act.

I would be inclined to make the same criticism on that. It is very easy to say ' shall be liable for a violation of this Act unless he shall prove that the person acting on his behalf did so against his express orders or direction.'

I think the section practically throws the

onus of proof on tlie person in charge of the business, whose subordinate may have sold the goods. The onus of proof is thrown on the principal to show that he was not personally responsible or guilty. This is the form adopted in several other Acts.
Section agreed to.

I wish to move that the following subsection be added :-
Any person who sells seed by wholesale in sealed packages, sacks or bags, to a retail vendor, shall not be liable for such seeds after the seal has been broken, unless such seal has been broken and a sample for official test is taken and inclosed in the sealed package in the presence of two iron-interested witnesses.
That is for the purpose of protecting the *wholesale dealer.

Amendment agreed to, and section as amended, agreed to.
On section 9,
I would like to ask the hon. minister what a man has to do when the seeds are on railway premises ? Suppose the seeds are in a locked car, will the officer have a right to break the lock open ?
He would have to appeal to the officer of the railway company, I imagine, to open the car. and if the officer refused, he would have authority under this to break open the car.
I suppose the officer of the department would carry his authority with him and be able to show it to anybody who required it ?
Who is going to s?e to the enforcement of this law ? Is the government going to appoint officers all over the country ?
There is no such intention.
It says ' Any person charged with the enforcement of this Act.' There must be some person charged. Who will it be ?

The present intention is that any officer of the department as at present constituted who may wish to take samples, or who may have reason to suspect that adulterated or impure seeds are being sold, will have authority to take samples.
Does the hon. minister mean the department here in Ottawa ?
Yes.
That is a sample of the whole Bill-unworkable.

Not at all.
On section 10-samples to be sent to official seed analyst. [DOT]
Is it proposed to appoint a special seed analyst ?
I have already an officer in the seed laboratory. This is a part of the work.

If we are going to have the thorough investigation we expect, thousands and tens of thousands of samples will be coming from all over the country. The analyst, in that case, is not going to be able to do all the work.
If samples come in in great numbers, we must increase the staff of the laboratory. But that will show how necessary and justifiable is the law.
Would it not be better to say plainly in the law to what inspector the seed shall be sent ?
They will be sent to the seed analyst.
Is he appointed ?

He is an officer of my department who is doing the work. But he would have to be appointed seed analyst by Order in Council. It says : ' Such person as the Governor in Council appoints as an official seed analyst.'
On section 11-sample to be taken in presence of sellers or two witnesses, certificate to accompany sample.
How will these samples be sent in, by post ?
Yes.
Free ?

Yes. The official seed analyst will be an officer of the department, and these would come to the department free under the Postal Act.
On section 12-samples to be sent within seven days.
Mr. SPttOULE. Suppose samples are not sent within the proper time, would that relieve the person selling the seed from any liability under the Act or prosecution for damages ?

I do not think it would free him from an action for damages, but it would free him

from penalties under this Act. X think there is no doubt about that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Fisher proposes to amend this section by adding to it the words ' in default whereof no prosecution shall lie with respect to such deeds.'

That might cover the point raised by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule). I think it would be better to leave that out.
On section 14-certificates of analysis as evidence,
Ought the minister not make some specific provisions for sealing up and sending in the seed ?

I propose to submit regulations and rules for the taking of these samples, and the provisions the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) refers to will be included in these. Section 18 allows for that.
On section 15,
Any pecuniary penalty imposed under this Act shall, on recovery be payable one-half to the informant or complainant, and the other half to His Majesty.

1 think that is objectionable-that a man should Be able to come into your house or store and be able to prosecute, half the fine going to him. I think the fine should all go to the Crown under the circumstances of this case. I think under all circumstances the fine should go to the Crown.

I may say that the seed merchants who have approached me on this Bill, have objected to this clause, and I am quite willing to strike it out.
On section 17,
Do I understand that there can be no appeal to the county judge in the province of Ontario ?

I am not familiar with the nomenclature of the different courts of the province of Ontario. This clause as well as the other clauses, in regard to legal proceedings, have been taken from the General Inspection Act, which I presume provided for the courts in the different provinces.
In Ontario the appeals from magistrates are always to the county court judges.

In the province of Quebec we have both a superior and a circuit court, so if you do not mention the court to which appeal is to be taken, we shall not know where to go. I think we should determine that in Quebec the appeal should be brought before the circuit court, because if brought before a superior court, the amount of costs
might be very large and the sum involved very small.

If the committee would allow, I would ask that that clause be allowed to stand for the opinion of the Minister of Justice.
Progress reported.

G. Blair) has tendered his resignation. It is openly stated, as my hon. friend is no doubt aware, throughout the corridors of the House, that such an event has taken place. maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-RESIGNATION OF HON. MR. BLAIR-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.

As to the business to be taken up to-morrow, we may be able to take one Or two Bills on the Order Paper at an early stage, and then we will ask the House to go into Committee of Supply, resuming consideration of the estimates of the Department of the Interior.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-RESIGNATION OF HON. MR. BLAIR-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-RESIGNATION OF HON. MR. BLAIR-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: Perhaps before to-morrow evening my hon. friend may be able to get into communication with the Prime Minister or the Minister of Railways I do not think there will be any great difficulty on the subject. I appreciate the fact that perhaps he has not been very anxious to meet them this evening, and under the circumstances I accept his explanation as the best he could offer.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-RESIGNATION OF HON. MR. BLAIR-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
